lessons.title: Tree structure and edges
lessons.summary: A rooted tree is connected and acyclic; only the root has no parent.
lessons.body:
Arrays and linked lists are **linear**: every element has at most one successor. A **tree** lets an element have several successors, which is exactly the shape of a lot of real data: a file system, the HTML DOM, an organisation chart, a parsed expression, a JSON document.

Trees also matter for speed. In this module, n is the number of items (keys or nodes) stored, and O(…) is Big O notation: it describes how the work grows as n grows. O(n) is a linear upper growth bound; O(log n) is a logarithmic upper growth bound using the base-2 logarithm of n, roughly the number of times you can halve n before reaching 1 (about 20 for a million). O(1) means a fixed amount of work however large n is.

A sorted array lets you search in O(log n) but inserts cost O(n), because every later item must shift along. A balanced binary search tree gives O(log n) search and insertion under constant-cost key comparisons: its height is logarithmic, and those operations follow a root-to-leaf path. An arbitrary well-shaped tree does not provide ordered search.

## What makes something a tree

A tree is a set of **nodes** joined by **edges**, with one special node, the **root node**, such that:

- every node except the root has exactly one **parent node**;
- following parents from any node always leads back to the root;
- there are no cycles.

Equivalently (in graph terms) a tree is a connected undirected graph with no cycles, with a root chosen for the rooted representation.

Because every node except the root has exactly one edge up to its parent, you can count the edges of any tree without looking at its shape:

```formula essential
E = n − 1
where
n: the number of nodes in the tree, a whole number of at least 1
E: the number of edges (parent–child links) in the tree
In words: a nonempty tree always has exactly one edge fewer than it has nodes, because the root is the only node with no edge to a parent.
```

So the tree below, with 8 nodes, has **7 edges**, and a tree of a million nodes has 999,999, whatever its shape. The rule needs a single connected tree; a collection of separate trees (a forest) has fewer edges.

The count is also a quick diagnostic. If a structure that should be a tree has as many links as nodes, something has a second parent or the links loop back on themselves. If it has fewer, part of it is disconnected from the root. The right count alone does not prove a tree, though: a loop in one part and a disconnected piece elsewhere can also add up to n − 1 links.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a company org chart
> In a strict org chart, the chief executive reports to nobody and every other employee reports to exactly one manager. Ask any employee who their manager is, then that manager, and you always end at the chief executive.
>
> **How it maps:** the chief executive is the root, each manager is a parent node, each reporting line is an edge, and staff with no reports are leaves. Because everyone except the chief executive has exactly one line upwards, a company of 250 people has 249 reporting lines however the departments are arranged.
>
> **Where it stops:** real organisations often have dotted-line reporting, where someone answers to two managers. That gives a node two parents, so the chart is no longer a tree. A data-structure tree also has no job titles: the only thing that matters is who links to whom.

```
            A          <- root (depth 0)
          / | \
         B  C  D       <- depth 1
        / \     \
       E   F     G     <- depth 2
           |
           H           <- depth 3
```

## Where trees appear

- **File systems**: a directory hierarchy is often modelled as a tree; empty directories are also leaves, and hard links or followed symbolic links need extra care.
- **Compilers**: source code is parsed into an *abstract syntax tree*; `(2 + 3) * 4` becomes a `*` node with children `+` and `4`.
- **Databases**: many indexes use B-trees, a many-children generalisation of search trees (covered in the System Design databases module).
- **Ordered maps**: Java's TreeMap uses a red-black tree; common std::map implementations do too, but the C++ interface does not require that representation (the balanced-tree units).
- **Schedulers and priority queues**: binary heaps (the binary heap units).
- **Autocomplete and routing tables**: tries (the trie units).

## Key takeaways
- A rooted tree is connected and acyclic; only the root has no parent.
- A nonempty tree has one fewer edge than nodes.
- Ordered search requires an ordering rule as well as a useful shape.

## Further reading
- [Tree (data structure) — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tree_(data_structure))
- [Binary expression tree — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_expression_tree)

questions.prompt: An HR import builds an org chart for a company of 250 people and is supposed to produce a tree: one chief executive at the root, and everyone else reporting to exactly one manager. A validation script counts **250 reporting lines** (edges). What does that tell you?

options.text: It is a valid tree: one reporting line per person
options.explanation: A tree needs one edge fewer than nodes. The chief executive is the root and has no line upwards, so a valid 250-person chart has 249 lines, not 250.

options.text: It is not a valid tree: someone has a second manager, or the lines form a loop
options.explanation: Correct. A connected tree of 250 nodes has exactly 249 edges. One extra edge means some person has two managers, or a chain of reporting lines loops back on itself; either breaks the tree rules.

options.text: Nothing yet: the edge count depends on how wide or deep the chart is
options.explanation: Shape changes the height and the number of leaves, but not the edge count. Every tree with 250 nodes has exactly 249 edges, so 250 is already a warning sign.

options.text: The chart is missing some people, so it has too few nodes
options.explanation: Missing people would remove nodes and their reporting lines together. A tree with fewer people would have fewer edges, not an extra one.

questions.workedExample:
1. In a tree, every node except the root has exactly one parent, and each parent link is one edge.
2. So a tree with 250 people has one edge per non-root person: 249 edges, whatever the chart's shape. A flat chart with 249 direct reports and a single chain of 250 people both have 249.
3. The import produced 250 edges, one too many. The extra link must give someone a second manager or close a loop of reporting lines, so the result is not a tree.
4. The fix is to find the person with two upward links, or the cycle, before any tree algorithm runs on the data.

lessons.title: Depth, height and recursive counting
lessons.summary: Depth looks upwards to the root; height looks down to the deepest leaf.
lessons.body:
Use the rooted-tree vocabulary from the earlier unit. The linked examples below assume a finite acyclic tree without shared child nodes. Count height and depth in edges, not nodes. A path ends at a leaf only when that node has no children. When an example uses n, it means the number of stored nodes.

## Vocabulary

| Term | Meaning (in the tree-structure unit’s A–H example) |
|---|---|
| Child / parent | B is a child of A; A is B's parent |
| Siblings | B, C and D share a parent |
| Leaf | A node with no children: E, H, C, G |
| Internal node | Has at least one child: A, B, F, D |
| Subtree | A node plus all its descendants |
| Ancestor | A, B and F are ancestors of H |
| Degree | Number of children (A has 3) |

### Depth versus height

These two are easy to mix up because they both count edges, but they look in opposite directions.

- The **node depth** of a node is the number of edges from the **root down to it**. The root has depth 0; H has depth 3.
- The **node height** of a node is the number of edges on the **longest path down to a leaf**. Leaves have height 0; B has height 2; A has height 3.
- The **height of the tree** is the height of its root, which equals the maximum depth of any node.

> [!warning] Conventions vary
> Some books count nodes rather than edges, so a single node has height 1 instead of 0. This module counts **edges**: a one-node tree has height 0 and an empty tree has height −1. Always check which convention a problem uses before you answer "what is the height?".

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: generations in a family tree
> Pick one family's founding ancestor. Your generation number is how many generations you sit below that ancestor. Separately, ask how many generations of descendants you have below you: none if you have no children, three if you have a great-grandchild.
>
> **How it maps:** the founding ancestor is the root. Your generation number is your depth, counted from the top down to you. The number of generations below you, along your longest line of descendants, is your height. A childless person is a leaf, with height 0.
>
> **Where it stops:** real people have two parents, so a full ancestry chart is not a tree at all; this picture follows only one line of descent. Families also often number the founder as "generation 1", which is the node-counting convention this module avoids.

### Computing height recursively

Height has a neat recursive definition: the height of a node is one more than the taller of its children's heights, and an empty subtree has height −1 so that a leaf comes out as 0. In the A–H tree, E is a leaf (height 0), F's only child H is a leaf, so F has height 1, and B is one more than the taller of E and F: height 2, matching the count by eye.

The recursion has to know both children's heights before it can answer for their parent, so it naturally works bottom-up. It visits each of the n nodes once, so it takes O(n) time. Its call stack holds one frame for each node on the longest root-to-leaf path, plus one for the final call on an empty child. A balanced tree keeps that shallow, but a degenerate chain of thousands of nodes can hit the runtime's recursion limit (CPython's default limit is 1,000 frames).

The following binary Node stores each child reference explicitly. The sample builds a four-node tree; the height function below accepts this representation and returns 2 for that sample root. For a node with any number of children, take the maximum over all of them instead of just two.

```python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, val, left=None,
                 right=None):
        self.val = val
        # Keep left/right
        # positions distinct.
        self.left = left
        self.right = right

#      1
#     / \
#    2   3
#   /
#  4
root = Node(1, Node(2, Node(4)), Node(3))
```

```python
def height(node):
    if node is None:
        return -1          # empty tree
    # Combine both child heights.
    return 1 + max(height(node.left),
                   height(node.right))
```

## Key takeaways
- Depth looks upwards to the root; height looks down to the deepest leaf.
- This module counts edges: leaves have height zero and empty trees height minus one.
- Recursive height combines children before their parent.

## Further reading
- [Tree (data structure) — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tree_(data_structure))
- [Binary tree — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_tree)

questions.prompt:
In the tree below, what are the **depth of T** and the **height of R**? (Count edges.)

```
        P
       / \
      Q   R
     /   / \
    S   T   U
         \
          V
```

options.text: T depth: 1, R height: 2
options.explanation: T is two edges below the root (P to R to T), not one. Depth counts edges from the root, and R is the node at depth 1.

options.text: T depth: 2, R height: 1
options.explanation: Depth is right, but the height of R is not 1: the longest downward path from R is R to T to V, which is 2 edges. Height 1 is the height of T.

options.text: T depth: 2, R height: 2
options.explanation: Correct. P to R to T is 2 edges, so T has depth 2. The longest path down from R is R to T to V, 2 edges, so R has height 2.

options.text: T depth: 3, R height: 3
options.explanation: This counts nodes rather than edges for both: P, R, T is three nodes but two edges. The lesson's convention counts edges.

questions.workedExample:
Depth looks **up** to the root; height looks **down** to the deepest leaf.

1. Depth of T: walk from the root, P to R (1 edge), R to T (2 edges). The depth is 2.
2. Height of R: list R's downward paths.
   - R to U: 1 edge.
   - R to T to V: 2 edges.
   The longest is 2, so R’s height is 2.
3. Sanity check: the whole tree's height is the deepest depth, which is V at depth 3. It also equals one more than the height of R, the taller child of the root P: 1 + 2 = 3.

questions.prompt:
Using the lesson's `height` function (which returns −1 for `None`), what does `height(root)` return here?

```python
root = Node(1,
            Node(2, Node(4)),
            Node(3))
```

options.explanation: This is the height of node 2 (2 to 4), not of the root. You need one more edge to get from the root down to node 2.
This counts nodes on the longest path (1, 2, 4). The function counts edges, so the answer is one less.
Correct. Nodes 4 and 3 are leaves (height 0) and node 2 has height 1, so the root's height is 1 plus the larger of 1 and 0, which is 2.
0 is the height of a single leaf. The root has descendants, so its height is larger.

questions.workedExample:
Evaluate bottom-up, starting from the leaves. Each node's height is one more than its taller child's height, and an empty child (None) counts as −1, so a leaf comes out as 0.

1. Node 4 has no children: 1 + max(−1, −1) = 0.
2. Node 3 has no children: also 0.
3. Node 2 has left child 4 (height 0) and no right child (−1): 1 + 0 = 1.
4. The root, node 1, has children 2 (height 1) and 3 (height 0): 1 + 1 = **2**.

Check by eye: the longest root-to-leaf path is 1 to 2 to 4, which is two edges.

questions.prompt:
What does this code print?

```python
def f(n):
    # Handle a missing child first.
    if n is None:
        return 0
    if not n.left and not n.right:
        return 1
    # Combine both subtree leaf counts.
    return f(n.left) + f(n.right)

root = Node(1,
  Node(2, Node(4), Node(5)),
  Node(3, None, Node(6)))
print(f(root))
```

options.explanation: 6 is the total number of nodes. The function only returns 1 for nodes with no children; internal nodes just pass along their children's sums.
Correct. f counts leaves. The leaves are 4, 5 and 6; nodes 1, 2 and 3 all have at least one child.
This would count node 3 as a leaf, but it has a right child (6). A leaf needs both children to be None.
This misses 6, perhaps by assuming a node with a None left child stops the recursion. The None branch returns 0 but the right branch is still explored.

questions.workedExample:
Trace the recursion from the leaves up. f returns 0 for None, 1 for a node with no children, and otherwise adds its two children's results.

1. Nodes 4 and 5 are leaves, so each returns 1, and node 2 returns 1 + 1 = 2.
2. Node 3 has no left child (that call returns 0) and a right child 6, which is a leaf and returns 1. So node 3 returns 0 + 1 = 1. The None branch does not stop the right branch being explored.
3. The root returns 2 + 1 = **3**.

Only leaves ever contribute 1; internal nodes just pass their children's totals upwards. So f counts leaves, and this tree's leaves are 4, 5 and 6.

lessons.title: Binary nodes and counting bounds
lessons.summary: Left and right child positions are distinct, even with only one child.
lessons.body:
Use the rooted-tree vocabulary from the earlier unit. The linked examples below assume a finite acyclic tree without shared child nodes. Count height and depth in edges, not nodes. A path ends at a leaf only when that node has no children. When an example uses n, it means the number of stored nodes.

## Binary trees

A **binary tree** is a tree where every node has at most two children, called **left** and **right**. The order matters: a node with only a left child is a different tree from one with only a right child.

Binary trees are the workhorse of this module. Binary search trees, AVL trees, red-black trees and binary heaps have binary shape. Other priority queue structures, such as d-ary heaps, allow higher arity, and expression trees can have unary or many-operand nodes.

Use the Node representation from the depth-and-height unit; the four-node example there also illustrates these child-slot counts.


Two useful counting facts.

### Empty child slots

Every node has two child slots, and every edge fills exactly one of them. A tree with n nodes has n − 1 edges, so the remaining slots, one more than the number of nodes, are empty (None):

```formula reference
S = 2n − (n − 1) = n + 1
where
S: the number of empty (None) child slots in a nonempty binary tree
n: the number of nodes
In words: a binary tree always has one more empty child slot than it has nodes.
```

In the four-node sample from the depth-and-height unit, node 4 has two empty slots, node 3 has two and node 2 has one: 5 in total. This is why serialising a tree with a marker for every empty child writes one more marker than nodes (the common-problem units).

### How short a tree can be

Each level can hold at most twice as many nodes as the level above it: 1 root, then at most 2, 4, 8 and so on. So every extra level roughly doubles how many nodes can fit, and the shortest possible tree grows only logarithmically. At the other extreme, nothing stops a badly shaped tree from being a single chain, one node per level:

```formula essential
h_min = ⌊log_2(n)⌋
h_max = n − 1
where
n: the number of nodes in the tree, at least 1
h_min: the smallest possible height, in edges, reached when every level except the last is full
h_max: the largest possible height, in edges, reached by a chain where every node has at most one child
log_2(n): the base-2 logarithm of n: how many times you can halve n before reaching 1, so log_2(8) = 3
⌊ ⌋: floor: round down to a whole number
In words: n nodes can be packed into a height of about log_2(n) edges, or strung out to a height of n − 1 edges; the shape decides which.
```

For a million nodes, that is a height somewhere between 19 and 999,999. Height 3 fits at most 15 nodes, height 9 up to 1,023, height 19 just over a million. Doubling the node count adds only one level to the shortest possible tree.

That gap is why "O(log n)" keeps appearing in this module. Operations that walk one root-to-leaf path take time proportional to the height, so a well-shaped tree reaches any node in about 20 steps per million nodes, while a chain behaves like a linked list.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a phone tree for news
> A club spreads news by phone. The organiser calls two people, each of them calls two more, and so on. With everyone passing it on, about 20 rounds of calls reach a million members. If instead each member calls just one other person, a million members need almost a million rounds.
>
> **How it maps:** each member is a node, each call is an edge and each round is one level. The two-calls-each scheme is a well-filled binary tree with logarithmic height; the one-call-each scheme is a chain with height one less than the number of nodes.
>
> **Where it stops:** a phone tree's job is to reach every member, so every call gets made. A tree lookup follows a single path from the root, one node per level, and skips everything else, so its cost is the height, not the total number of calls. Real callers also phone people one after another, so rounds are never perfectly simultaneous.

## Key takeaways
- Left and right child positions are distinct, even with only one child.
- Count empty slots by subtracting occupied edges from child positions.
- Doubling each level gives the shortest possible height for a node count: about log₂ n levels.
- A chain is the tallest possible shape, so shape, not node count, decides whether paths are short.

## Further reading
- [Binary tree — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_tree)

questions.prompt: A complete binary tree (every level full except possibly the last, which fills from the left) holds 1,000 nodes and has height 9. You keep adding nodes in the same complete shape until it holds 2,000. What happens to its height?

options.text: It roughly doubles, to about 18
options.explanation: Height would double only if each level held a fixed number of nodes. Here each level can hold twice as many as the one above, so doubling the nodes adds a level rather than doubling the height.

options.text: It stays at 9
options.explanation: Height 9 holds at most 1,023 nodes (levels of 1, 2, 4 … 512). Once the tree passes that, a new level must start.

options.text: It grows by exactly one level, to 10
options.explanation: Correct. Each new level can hold as many nodes as all the levels above it put together, plus one. Height 10 holds up to 2,047 nodes, so 2,000 nodes fit with just one extra level.

options.text: It grows by about 1,000, because each new node adds depth
options.explanation: That describes a chain where every node has one child. A complete tree fills each level across before starting the next one.

questions.workedExample:
1. In a binary tree, each level can hold at most twice as many nodes as the level above: 1, 2, 4, 8, … 512 for levels 0 to 9.
2. Those ten levels add up to 1,023, so a complete tree of 1,000 nodes has height 9: its last level is nearly full.
3. The next level, level 10, can hold another 1,024 nodes on its own. Adding 1,000 more nodes fills most of that one level, and the total of 2,000 is below the 2,047 that height 10 allows.
4. So the height goes from 9 to 10. Doubling the node count adds one level, which is what logarithmic height means in practice: about 20 levels for a million nodes, 30 for a billion.

questions.prompt: Two binary trees each hold 1,000 nodes. Tree X has height 9 and tree Y has height 999 (heights in edges). Which statement is right?

options.text: Y cannot hold only 1,000 nodes: a height of 999 needs more nodes than that
options.explanation: A tall tree does not need many nodes. A chain where every node has one child gains a level per node, so 1,000 nodes in a chain have height 999.

options.text: X must be a perfect tree, with every level completely full
options.explanation: A perfect tree of height 9 has exactly 1,023 nodes. X has 1,000, so its last level is not full; it can still be as short as possible, for example as a complete tree.

options.text: X is as short as any 1,000-node binary tree can be, and Y is a chain with one node per level
options.explanation: Correct. Height 8 can hold at most 511 nodes, so 9 is the minimum for 1,000 nodes. Height 999 is the maximum: every node has at most one child, so the tree is a chain.

options.text: Their heights differ, but a search that follows one root-to-leaf path takes about the same time in both
options.explanation: A path-following search costs time proportional to the height, so Y can take about 1,000 steps where X takes about 10. That gap is the whole reason balancing exists.

questions.workedExample:
1. Shortest possible: levels hold at most 1, 2, 4 … nodes, so height 8 fits at most 511 nodes and height 9 fits up to 1,023. 1,000 nodes need height at least 9, and X achieves it.
2. Tallest possible: a tree is tallest when it is a chain, one node per level. 1,000 nodes then span 999 edges, so Y must be a chain (each node has at most one child).
3. X need not be perfect: a perfect height-9 tree would hold 1,023 nodes, not 1,000.
4. Consequence: an operation that walks one root-to-leaf path visits at most 10 nodes in X but up to 1,000 in Y.

lessons.title: Full, complete, perfect and balanced
lessons.summary: Full describes child counts; complete describes filled positions.
lessons.body:
Use the rooted-tree vocabulary from the earlier unit. The linked examples below assume a finite acyclic tree without shared child nodes. Count height and depth in edges, not nodes. A path ends at a leaf only when that node has no children. When an example uses n, it means the number of stored nodes.

## Shapes: full, complete, perfect, balanced

These four words get confused constantly, and interviewers love them.

```
 Full        Complete    Perfect
   o            o           o
  / \          / \        /   \
 o   o        o   o      o     o
    / \      / \  /     / \   / \
   o   o    o  o o     o   o o   o
```

- **Full tree** (or *proper*): every node has **0 or 2 children**, never exactly one. A full binary tree always has one more leaf than internal node (see the formula below).
- **Complete tree**: every level is completely filled **except possibly the last**, and the last level is filled **from left to right** with no gaps. This is the shape a binary heap always has. (Some authors use "complete" for what this module calls perfect, so check the definition a source uses.)
- **Perfect tree**: every internal node has two children and **all leaves are at the same depth**. Every level is full, so it holds the maximum number of nodes for its height: 1, 3, 7, 15, 31... nodes for heights 0 to 4.
- **Height-balanced tree**: for every node, the heights of its left and right subtrees differ by **at most 1**. More loosely, people say a tree is balanced when its height is O(log n), where n counts nodes.

A full tree always has **exactly one more leaf than internal nodes**. Count its edges two ways: each internal node owns exactly two child edges, and any tree has one edge fewer than nodes. Those two counts only agree when the leaves outnumber the internal nodes by one:

```formula reference
L_f = i + 1
where
i: the number of internal nodes (nodes with children); each has exactly 2 children in a full tree
L_f: the number of leaves in the full binary tree
In words: every full binary tree has one more leaf than it has internal nodes, so its total node count is always odd.
```

The "Full" tree in the picture has two internal nodes and 3 leaves. A knockout tournament is the same shape: 16 players (leaves) need exactly 15 matches (internal nodes), however the draw is arranged.

The balance rule is a check you make at **every** node, not just the root. Using this module's edge-counted heights, an empty subtree has height −1. So a node whose left child has a child of its own (left height 1) but whose right side is empty (height −1) is out of balance by 2, and the tree is not height-balanced even if every other node is fine.

Every perfect tree is both full and complete, but the other combinations are independent. In the picture, the "Full" tree is full but **not complete**: its last level is filled on the right with a gap on the left. The "Complete" tree is complete but **not full**: the right child of the root has only one child.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: seating an audience row by row
> An usher fills a theatre from the front row, left to right, and starts a new row only when the current one is full. At any moment every row is full except the one being filled, and that row has no gaps on its left.
>
> **How it maps:** rows are levels and seats are node positions. The usher's rule produces exactly a complete tree. A completely sold-out theatre with every row full corresponds to a perfect tree.
>
> **Where it stops:** in a tree, each level has twice as many seats as the one above, and every seat must sit under an occupied seat in the row before. The analogy also says nothing about "full", which is a rule about each node's child count, not about filling order.

> [!tip] Why shape matters
> Ordered searches and single-key updates in a balanced BST cost time proportional to the height; traversing all n nodes takes O(n). A complete tree with a million nodes has height 19; other balancing rules permit larger logarithmic heights. A degenerate one, where each node has a single child, has height 999,999 and is just a slow linked list.

## Key takeaways
- Full describes child counts; complete describes filled positions.
- Perfect requires every level to be full.
- Height balance must hold at every node, not just the root.

## Further reading
- [Binary tree — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_tree)

questions.prompt:
Which descriptions apply to this binary tree? Select all that apply.

```
       o
      / \
     o   o
    / \
   o   o
```

options.text: Full
options.explanation: Correct. Every node has either 0 or 2 children: the root has 2, its left child has 2, and the other three are leaves.

options.text: Complete
options.explanation: Correct. Levels 0 and 1 are completely filled, and the last level's two nodes are packed to the left with no gap.

options.text: Perfect
options.explanation: Not perfect: the leaves are at different depths (the root's right child is a leaf at depth 1, the others are at depth 2). A perfect tree of height 2 would have 7 nodes.

options.text: Height-balanced
options.explanation: Correct. At the root, the left subtree has height 1 and the right has height 0, a difference of 1. Every other node's subtrees differ by 0.

questions.workedExample:
Check each definition against each node.

1. **Full tree** (0 or 2 children everywhere): root 2, left child 2, three leaves 0. Yes.
2. **Complete tree** (all levels full except the last, which fills left to right): level 0 has 1/1, level 1 has 2/2, level 2 has its 2 nodes in the two leftmost positions. Yes.
3. **Perfect tree** (all leaves at the same depth): leaves at depths 1, 2 and 2. No. A perfect tree of height 2 has 7 nodes; this has 5.
4. **Height-balanced**: at the root, heights are 1 (left) and 0 (right), difference 1. At the left child, 0 and 0. Leaves trivially balance. Yes.

questions.prompt: A colleague's unit test builds a **full** binary tree (every node has 0 or 2 children) and asserts that it contains exactly **20 nodes**. The test keeps failing. What is the most likely problem?

options.text: The tree must also be complete before it can be full
options.explanation: Full and complete are independent: a full tree may have gaps on its last level. Completeness has nothing to do with this count.

options.text: A full binary tree must have a power of two minus one nodes (1, 3, 7, 15, 31 …)
options.explanation: That is the rule for a perfect tree, where every level is full. A full tree can have, for example, 5 nodes: a root, one leaf child and one child with two leaves.

options.text: Nothing structural: a full binary tree with 20 nodes is fine, so the bug must be elsewhere
options.explanation: A full binary tree cannot have 20 nodes. It always has one more leaf than internal nodes, so its total is twice the internal count plus one: always odd.

options.text: The expected count is impossible: every full binary tree has an odd number of nodes
options.explanation: Correct. In a full tree each internal node owns exactly two edges, and any tree has one edge fewer than nodes. That forces one more leaf than internal node, so the total is always odd; 20 can never be right.

questions.workedExample:
1. In a full binary tree, every internal node has exactly two children, so the edges number twice the internal nodes.
2. Any tree has one edge fewer than it has nodes.
3. Putting those together, the node count is twice the internal count plus one. Equivalently, there is always exactly one more leaf than internal node.
4. Twice anything plus one is odd, so a full binary tree can have 19 or 21 nodes but never 20. The test's expectation is wrong (or the tree it builds is not full).

The same fact explains a knockout tournament: 16 players are the leaves and the 15 matches are the internal nodes.

questions.prompt: Which of these statements are always true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Every perfect binary tree is also complete
options.explanation: Correct. A perfect tree has every level completely filled, which trivially satisfies 'all levels full except possibly the last, filled left to right'.

options.text: Every complete binary tree is height-balanced
options.explanation: Correct. In a complete tree, every node's left subtree is at most one level taller than its right, because only the last level can be partial and it fills from the left.

options.text: Every height-balanced tree is complete
options.explanation: False. A balanced tree can have gaps on its last level (for example a root with only a right child), which breaks the left-to-right filling rule of completeness.

options.text: Every full binary tree is complete
options.explanation: False. A full tree can grow deep on one side only, such as a root whose right child has two children while its left child is a leaf; the left gap breaks completeness.

options.text: A full binary tree always has an odd number of nodes
options.explanation: Correct. It has twice as many nodes as it has internal nodes, plus one, which is always odd.

questions.workedExample:
Test each claim with a definition or a counter-example.

1. Perfect implies complete: every level full is the strongest possible case of 'levels full, last one left-packed'. True.
2. Complete implies balanced: at any node, both subtrees are complete and their heights differ by at most 1 (the left can reach one level deeper only into the partial last level). True.
3. Balanced implies complete? Counter-example: a root with only a right child. Heights −1 and 0 differ by 1, so it is balanced, but the missing left child is a gap. False.
4. Full implies complete? Counter-example from the source example's 'Full' diagram: leaf on the left, two children on the right. False.
5. Full implies odd: the total is twice the number of internal nodes plus one (each internal node owns two edges, and there is one more node than edges). True.

lessons.title: Linked nodes, arrays and parent pointers
lessons.summary: Arrays suit complete trees and calculate child positions without links.
lessons.body:
Use the rooted-tree vocabulary from the earlier unit. The linked examples below assume a finite acyclic tree without shared child nodes. Count height and depth in edges, not nodes. A path ends at a leaf only when that node has no children. When an example uses n, it means the number of stored nodes.

## Representing trees in memory

### Linked nodes

The usual choice: each node is an object with a value and pointers to its children (and sometimes its parent). It handles any shape. Relinking a known subtree can change only a few pointers, but locating it, maintaining metadata or balancing, and reclaiming removed nodes can require additional work.

The cost is memory and cache behaviour. Every node carries its child pointers and, in languages like Python, an object header as well, so a tree of small values can use several times more memory than the values themselves. For example, on 64-bit CPython 3.14 each object of a plain node class with a value and two child fields takes about 100 bytes, not counting the value it refers to; exact sizes depend on the language, version and class layout. Nodes allocated separately can end up scattered in memory, which can make traversals slower than walking an array, although it does not mean a cache miss on every visit.

### Arrays (implicit trees)

A **complete binary tree** can be stored in a plain array with no pointers at all. Put the nodes in level order (the root, then each level left to right), numbering slots from 0:

```
 index:  0  1  2  3  4  5
 value: [A, B, C, D, E, F]

        A(0)
       /    \
     B(1)    C(2)
    /  \     /
  D(3) E(4) F(5)
```

Arithmetic on the index then replaces the pointers:

```formula essential
i_left = 2i + 1
i_right = 2i + 2
i_parent = ⌊(i − 1) / 2⌋
where
i: the index (0-based array position) of a node; i_parent applies only when i > 0, since the root at index 0 has no parent
i_left: the index of that node's left child
i_right: the index of that node's right child
i_parent: the index of that node's parent
⌊ ⌋: floor: round down to a whole number, so ⌊1.5⌋ = 1
In words: the children of slot i sit at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, and you get back to the parent by subtracting 1, halving and rounding down.
```

So B at index 1 has its left child D at index 3, and F at index 5 has its parent C at index 2. A child index that falls past the end of the array means that child is missing. In Python the same arithmetic is `2*i + 1`, `2*i + 2` and `(i - 1) // 2`, where `//` divides and rounds down.

This is compact and cache-friendly, and it is exactly how binary heaps are implemented (the binary heap units). Because a complete tree has no gaps, every slot from 0 to n − 1 is used and nothing else is needed.

It wastes space badly for sparse, unbalanced trees, since a missing node still needs a slot. Follow a chain that only ever goes right: each step to a right child roughly doubles the index, so a 4-node chain sits at indices 0, 2, 6 and 14 and needs 15 slots to store 4 values. Every node added to the chain roughly doubles the array again, so the implicit layout is a poor fit for any shape that is not close to complete.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: numbered plots on a planned estate
> Imagine an estate where plots are numbered by a fixed rule: plot 0 is at the entrance, the two plots that branch off it are 1 and 2, the two off plot 1 are 3 and 4, and so on. To find a neighbour you never need directions; you work the number out.
>
> **How it maps:** a plot number is an array index, the numbering rule is the child and parent arithmetic, and needing no directions is having no pointers. A plot with no house still keeps its number, just as a missing child still reserves an array slot.
>
> **Where it stops:** the arithmetic only stays cheap if the plots are filled in order with no gaps. Real estates, like linked trees, can grow anywhere; an implicit tree cannot add a node in the middle without moving others.

### Trees with many children

For nodes with an unbounded number of children (a file system, the DOM), store a **list of children** per node. An older trick is **left-child, right-sibling**: each node keeps a pointer to its first child and one to its next sibling, which turns any tree into a binary tree.

```python
class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        self.children = []   # any number
```

### Parent pointers

Adding a `parent` field makes it easy to walk upwards (to find an in-order successor, or the path to the root) at the cost of one more pointer per node and more bookkeeping on every change. Red-black trees in the Linux kernel and in common C++ standard-library implementations keep parent pointers for this reason.

## Key takeaways
- Arrays suit complete trees and calculate child positions without links.
- Sparse chains waste exponentially many slots in the implicit layout.
- Linked nodes and child lists accommodate irregular shapes.

## Further reading
- [Tree (data structure) — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tree_(data_structure))
- [Binary tree — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_tree)

lessons.title: Recursive traversal orders
lessons.summary: Pre-order handles parents first; post-order handles children first.
lessons.body:
A list has one natural order: front to back. A tree does not. To visit every node you must decide, at each node, whether to handle the node itself before, between or after its children, and whether to go **deep** first or **wide** first.

Those choices give the four traversals you will use constantly. Each emits every node once; with constant-cost node processing and suitable stack/queue operations, these implementations take O(n) time, where n is the number of nodes: the work grows in direct proportion to the size of the tree. Assume finite acyclic binary trees without shared subtrees or concurrent mutation. They differ in the order of visits and in how much extra memory they need.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: reading and costing a report outline
> A report has chapters, each with sections and subsections. To print its table of contents you write each heading before the headings inside it. To work out the total page count you must first know every subsection's pages, add them into each section, then into each chapter.
>
> **How it maps:** the report is a tree of headings. Writing a heading before its contents is pre-order, the parent-first order. Adding up page counts from the bottom is post-order, the children-first order, because a parent's answer depends on its children's answers.
>
> **Where it stops:** headings can have any number of children, while in-order, "left, node, right", only makes sense for binary trees. A report is also read in one fixed order, whereas a traversal is a choice you make to suit the job.

## The running example

```
          F
        /   \
       B     G
      / \     \
     A   D     I
        / \   /
       C   E H
```

| Traversal | Order | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Pre-order | node, left, right | F B A D C E G I H |
| In-order | left, node, right | A B C D E F G H I |
| Post-order | left, right, node | A C E D B H I G F |
| Level-order | level by level | F B G A D I C E H |

This tree happens to be a binary search tree, which is why in-order comes out alphabetical. That is not a coincidence (see below).

## Depth-first: pre, in and post-order

The three depth-first traversals have identical structure; only the position of the "visit" line moves.

```python
def preorder(node, out):
    if node is None:
        return
    # Record this node at this position.
    out.append(node.val)       # visit
    preorder(node.left, out)
    preorder(node.right, out)

def inorder(node, out):
    if node is None:
        return
    inorder(node.left, out)
    # Record this node at this position.
    out.append(node.val)       # visit
    inorder(node.right, out)

def postorder(node, out):
    if node is None:
        return
    postorder(node.left, out)
    postorder(node.right, out)
    # Record this node at this position.
    out.append(node.val)       # visit
```

A trick for doing them by hand: walk round the outline of the tree anticlockwise starting at the root, keeping the tree on your left. Pre-order records a node when you pass its **left** side, in-order when you pass **underneath** it, post-order when you pass its **right** side.

### What each order is for

- **Pre-order** sees a parent before its children. Use it to copy or serialise a tree, including null markers or other shape metadata when reconstruction is required; the root-first order supports top-down rebuilding, and to print indented outlines such as a directory listing.
- **In-order** on a binary search tree yields keys in **sorted order**. Use it to validate a BST, find the k-th smallest key or range-scan.
- **Post-order** sees children before their parent. Use it whenever a node's answer depends on its subtrees: computing **node height** or size, **freeing** memory (delete children before the parent), evaluating an **expression tree** (`3 4 +` is post-order for `3 + 4`), or `rm -r` and `du` on a directory.

> [!tip] Most tree problems are post-order
> "Compute something for every subtree and combine" (height, diameter, balanced check, max path sum) is post-order: recurse into both children, then combine their results at the node. The common-problem units is full of these.

### Space: the hidden cost

Recursion is not free. Each pending call sits on the call stack, and at any moment the stack holds one frame for each node on the path from the root down to where the traversal currently is, plus one for a call on an empty child. So the deepest the stack gets is set by the tree's **height**, not by its number of nodes.

For a million-node complete tree that is about 21 frames: the height is 19. For a million nodes in a single chain it is about a million frames. In Big O terms, with h the height in edges, depth-first traversal needs O(h + 1) working space, excluding the O(n) output: O(log n) for a balanced tree but **O(n) for a degenerate one**.

CPython commonly starts with a recursion limit of 1,000; query sys.getrecursionlimit() for the actual process. A sufficiently deep chain raises RecursionError, accounting for existing call depth. Raising the limit can create resource risks; an iterative traversal avoids recursive call-depth limits but still needs memory.

## Key takeaways
- Pre-order handles parents first; post-order handles children first.
- In-order yields sorted values only when the tree has BST ordering.
- Recursive working memory grows with height; stored output grows with node count.

## Further reading
- [Tree traversal — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tree_traversal)

lessons.title: Explicit stacks for depth-first traversal
lessons.summary: A LIFO stack reverses the order in which children are pushed.
lessons.body:
Use the binary Node representation introduced earlier: each node has a value and optional left and right children. Assume finite acyclic trees without shared nodes or concurrent mutation. Here n counts nodes and h is the root height in edges. Constant-cost processing at each visited node is assumed; returned output is separate from working memory.

## Iterative depth-first traversals

Replace the call stack with an explicit list used as a stack.

### Pre-order

Pop a node, visit it, then push its children. Push the **right child first** so that the left is popped first.

```python
def preorder_iter(root):
    out = []
    stack = [root] if root else []
    while stack:
        node = stack.pop()
        out.append(node.val)
        # LIFO: right waits for left.
        if node.right:
            stack.append(node.right)
        if node.left:
            stack.append(node.left)
    return out
```

### In-order

Slide down to the leftmost node, stacking each ancestor on the way. Pop, visit, then repeat the slide from the popped node's right child.

```python
def inorder_iter(root):
    out, stack = [], []
    node = root
    while node or stack:
        while node:            # go left
            stack.append(node)
            node = node.left
        node = stack.pop()     # visit
        out.append(node.val)
        node = node.right      # then right
    return out
```

This pattern is worth memorising: it is also how you build a **BST iterator** that yields the next key on demand. Over a full traversal of n nodes each advance costs O(1) amortised (constant on average, because each node is pushed and popped once in total), and the stack needs O(h + 1) memory for a tree of height h. Initialisation or an individual next call can cost O(h + 1).

### Post-order

Post-order is the awkward one, because a node can only be visited after both children are done. The neat trick: do a pre-order that goes **node, right, left**, then reverse the output. Reversed, that is left, right, node.

```python
def postorder_iter(root):
    out = []
    stack = [root] if root else []
    while stack:
        node = stack.pop()
        out.append(node.val)
        if node.left:
            stack.append(node.left)
        # LIFO visits right before left.
        if node.right:
            stack.append(node.right)
    # Reverse node-right-left into
    # postorder.
    return out[::-1]
```

This uses O(n) memory for the output it reverses, for n nodes. If you need to *act* on nodes in post-order as you go (to free them, say), use the single-stack version that remembers the last node visited, so it can tell whether it is returning from the left or the right subtree.

## Key takeaways
- A LIFO stack reverses the order in which children are pushed.
- In-order keeps pending ancestors until their left side is finished.
- Reversing a right-first pre-order gives post-order output, with output storage.

## Further reading
- [Tree traversal — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tree_traversal)

lessons.title: Level order and queue width
lessons.summary: A deque processes the shallowest pending nodes first.
lessons.body:
Use the binary Node representation introduced earlier: each node has a value and optional left and right children. Assume finite acyclic trees without shared nodes or concurrent mutation. Here n counts nodes and h is the root height in edges. Constant-cost processing at each visited node is assumed; returned output is separate from working memory.

## Breadth-first: level-order

Level-order visits nodes by depth: the root, then all depth-1 nodes left to right, and so on. It uses a **queue** instead of a stack: first in, first out, so nodes are processed in the order they were discovered.

```python
from collections import deque

def level_order(root):
    if root is None:
        return []
    levels, q = [], deque([root])
    while q:
        level = []
        for _ in range(len(q)):
            node = q.popleft()
            # This round visits one fixed
            # depth.
            level.append(node.val)
            if node.left:
                q.append(node.left)
            if node.right:
                q.append(node.right)
        levels.append(level)
    return levels

# [['F'], ['B', 'G'],
#  ['A', 'D', 'I'], ['C', 'E', 'H']]
```

Taking `len(q)` at the start of each round processes exactly one level per round. That is the hook for a whole family of problems: right-side view (last of each level), zigzag order, average per level, minimum depth.

> [!warning] Use a deque, not a list
> `list.pop(0)` shifts every remaining element, so it is O(n) in the n items still in the list, and can make BFS quadratic (work growing with the square of the node count) on wide trees. `deque.popleft()` is O(1), a fixed cost.

### Space for BFS

The queue can mix the unprocessed part of one level with discovered nodes of the next, so its size grows with the tree's **tree width** (the most nodes on any one level), written O(width). In a perfect tree each level holds twice as many nodes as the one above, so the bottom level alone holds just over half of all the nodes. Once the level above it has been processed, every one of those leaves is waiting in the queue.

A perfect tree of 15 nodes has 8 leaves; one of 1,048,575 nodes has 524,288. So BFS uses O(n) memory on bushy trees, while DFS needs only O(log n) there. On a degenerate chain it is the other way round: the queue never holds more than one node, but recursive DFS needs O(n) frames. Iterative pre-order can keep only one pending node on a chain.

For n nodes:

| Shape | Recursive DFS stack | BFS queue |
|---|---|---|
| Balanced | O(log n) | O(n) |
| Chain | O(n) | O(1) |

BFS has one big advantage: it reaches shallow nodes first. To find the **minimum depth** of a tree, or the nearest node satisfying a condition, BFS can stop as soon as it finds one, while DFS might explore a huge deep subtree first.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: searching outwards street by street
> You want the nearest shop that sells a spare part. You check every shop one street away before any shop two streets away, keeping a list of the side streets still to visit. The first shop that has it is guaranteed to be one of the nearest.
>
> **How it maps:** streets away is depth, the list of side streets still to check is the queue, and checking in the order you wrote them down is first in, first out. Stopping at the first shop that has the part is how BFS finds the minimum depth without exploring far-away branches.
>
> **Where it stops:** in a bushy tree the "still to check" list becomes enormous, because each level is twice as wide as the one before. Depth-first search needs only enough memory for the current path, but it can wander far down one branch before trying a nearer one.

## Key takeaways
- A deque processes the shallowest pending nodes first.
- Snapshot the queue length before processing a level.
- Breadth-first working space can be large on wide trees.

## Further reading
- [Breadth-first search — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breadth-first_search)
- [collections.deque — Python docs](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.html)

lessons.title: Morris traversal and temporary threads
lessons.summary: Temporary predecessor links replace an explicit traversal stack.
lessons.body:
Use the binary Node representation introduced earlier: each node has a value and optional left and right children. Assume finite acyclic trees without shared nodes or concurrent mutation. Here n counts nodes and h is the root height in edges. Constant-cost processing at each visited node is assumed; returned output is separate from working memory.

## Advanced aside: Morris traversal

Can you do an in-order traversal with **O(1) extra space**, no stack and no recursion? Yes, if you are allowed to modify the tree temporarily.

Morris traversal (Joseph M. Morris, 1979) uses the empty right pointers of nodes as temporary **threads** back to their in-order successor:

1. If the current node has no left child, visit it and go right.
2. Otherwise, find its in-order predecessor (the rightmost node of its left subtree).
   - If the predecessor's right pointer is empty, point it at the current node (a thread) and go left.
   - If it already points at the current node, we have come back up via the thread: remove it, visit the current node and go right.

```python
def morris_inorder(root):
    out, cur = [], root
    while cur:
        if cur.left is None:
            out.append(cur.val)
            cur = cur.right
            continue
        pred = cur.left
        while (pred.right and
               pred.right is not cur):
            pred = pred.right
        if pred.right is None:
            # Save a route
            # back to this
            # ancestor.
            pred.right = cur   # thread
            cur = cur.left
        else:
            # Restore the
            # original empty
            # link.
            pred.right = None  # unthread
            out.append(cur.val)
            cur = cur.right
    return out
```

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: chalk marks in a maze
> Exploring a maze without a notebook, before you enter a side passage you find the last dead end you will reach in it and chalk an arrow there pointing back to the junction you are leaving. You then explore the passage. When you reach the arrow you follow it back to the junction, rub it out and carry on. You never need to remember the whole route, and the walls end up clean.
>
> **How it maps:** the junction is the current node, the last dead end in the side passage is its in-order predecessor (the rightmost node of its left subtree), the chalk arrow is the temporary thread in that node's empty right pointer, following it back replaces popping a stack, and rubbing it out is restoring the pointer to empty.
>
> **Where it stops:** anyone else in the maze sees your arrows and may follow them. If you leave halfway, the arrows stay on the walls; in the tree, that leaves cycles behind unless the walk is finished or the threads are removed.

Each edge is walked a constant number of times, so it is still **O(n) time** for n nodes. The catch is that the tree is temporarily rewired: it is unsafe if another thread is reading the tree concurrently, and if you stop early (say, on finding a key) you must still finish the walk or the threads stay in place. The O(1) bound excludes the output list: the shown function stores O(n) output. Exceptions or early exits also require cleanup of outstanding threads.

## Key takeaways
- Temporary predecessor links replace an explicit traversal stack.
- Remove each thread on the second encounter.
- Constant working space excludes output and requires safe cleanup.

## Further reading
- [Threaded binary tree (Morris traversal) — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Threaded_binary_tree)

options.text: It only works on binary search trees

options.text: It temporarily rewrites right pointers, so a concurrent reader can see a modified tree

2. Time: for each node with a left child, the walk to its predecessor goes down the right spine of its left subtree, once to create the thread and once to remove it. Each edge belongs to at most one such spine, so the total work is O(n).
3. Shape only: nothing compares keys, so any binary tree works.
4. Mutation: between threading and unthreading, some right pointers point *up* the tree. A concurrent reader, or a walk you abandon early, sees a tree with cycles.

lessons.title: BST ordering, search and insertion
lessons.summary: Ordering constrains entire subtrees, not only immediate children.
lessons.body:
Binary search on a sorted array of n keys finds a key in O(log n) steps (it halves the range each time, so about 20 steps for a million keys), but inserting a key means shifting everything after it: O(n), work in proportion to n. A **binary search tree** (BST) stores ordered partitions in linked nodes. A step need not halve the remaining keys; search follows a path, after which insertion or deletion relinks nodes.

When the tree is reasonably balanced, search, insert and delete are all **O(log n)**. When it is not, they degrade to O(n). Most of this lesson is about the operations; the later insertion-shape unit explains that failure mode, which the balanced-tree units address.

## The BST property

For **every** node:

- every key in its **left subtree** is **less** than the node's key;
- every key in its **right subtree** is **greater**.

The rule is about whole subtrees, not just immediate children. That distinction is where most BST bugs live (see the later successor-and-validation unit).

```
            50
          /    \
        30      70
       /  \    /  \
     20   40  60   80
         /  \   \
        35  45   65
```

An in-order traversal of this tree gives 20 30 35 40 45 50 60 65 70 80: a BST *is* a sorted sequence, stored as a tree.

Duplicates need a policy. The common choices are to reject them (sets and maps), keep a count in the node, or consistently send equal keys to one side. The code below ignores duplicates and assumes mutually comparable keys with a consistent total order, constant-cost comparisons and no concurrent mutation. Recursive functions are limited by Python call depth. Maps generally update an existing key rather than reject its new value.

## Search

Start at the root. If the key is smaller, go left; if larger, go right; stop when you find it or fall off the tree.

```python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, key):
        self.key = key
        self.left = self.right = None

def search(node, key):
    # Follow only the side containing
    # the key.
    while node and node.key != key:
        if key < node.key:
            node = node.left
        else:
            node = node.right
    return node        # None if absent
```

Searching for 45: 50 (go left), 30 (go right), 40 (go right), 45. Four nodes visited; the Python code can perform both equality and ordering tests at a node.

A search visits one node per level it passes through: one more node than the key's depth, and never more than the tree's height plus one. A miss walks a full path down to an empty child. So the cost depends on the tree's **height**, not directly on how many keys it holds: O(h + 1), where h is the height in edges. The minimum is the leftmost node and the maximum is the rightmost, found the same way.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a higher-or-lower guessing game
> A friend thinks of a number and you guess; after each guess they say "higher" or "lower", and you never need to consider the other side again. You find the number in a handful of guesses if each guess is near the middle of what is left.
>
> **How it maps:** each node's key is a guess, "lower" sends you to the left subtree and "higher" to the right, and the number of guesses is the number of nodes on the search path.
>
> **Where it stops:** in the game you choose a fresh middle guess each time. A BST's guesses are fixed by where earlier keys were inserted, so a badly shaped tree keeps guessing near one end and can need as many guesses as there are keys.

## Insert

Search for the key; the place where the search falls off the tree is exactly where the new key belongs. A new key always becomes a **leaf**.

```python
def insert(node, key):
    if node is None:
        return Node(key)
    if key < node.key:
        # Reconnect the returned
        # subtree root.
        node.left = insert(node.left, key)
    elif key > node.key:
        node.right = insert(node.right, key)
    return node        # duplicates ignored

root = None
for k in [50, 30, 70, 20, 40,
          60, 80, 35, 45, 65]:
    root = insert(root, k)
```

The recursive style "return the (possibly new) subtree root and reassign it" is worth adopting. It avoids special-casing the empty tree and is the same shape you need for delete and for balanced trees.

> [!note] Insertion order determines shape
> The same set of keys can produce very different trees. The order above gives the height-3 tree in the diagram. Inserting the same ten keys in ascending order gives a chain of height 9.

## Key takeaways
- Ordering constrains entire subtrees, not only immediate children.
- Search follows a single root-to-key path.
- Insertion returns a possibly new subtree root and ignores duplicate keys here.

## Further reading
- [Binary search tree — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_search_tree)
- [Binary Search Trees — Algorithms, 4th ed. (Sedgewick & Wayne)](https://algs4.cs.princeton.edu/32bst/)

lessons.title: Deleting leaves and internal BST nodes
lessons.summary: Remove a leaf, splice a single child, or substitute a two-child node.
lessons.body:
Earlier units established a strict BST ordering with distinct, mutually comparable keys: every left-subtree key is smaller and every right-subtree key larger. Use the Node with key, left and right fields introduced in the search unit. Here n counts keys and h measures tree height in edges. Comparisons have constant cost; recursive code remains limited by Python call depth.

## Delete: the three cases

Deletion is the operation people get wrong, because removing a node can leave a hole that must be filled without breaking the ordering. Find the node, then:

1. **No children (a leaf).** Just remove it. Deleting 20 sets 30's left pointer to None.
2. **One child.** Splice the child into the node's place. Deleting 60 makes 65 the left child of 70. Everything in 60's subtree was already between 50 and 70, so order is preserved.
3. **Two children.** You cannot splice two subtrees into one pointer. Instead, replace the node's key with its **in-order successor** (the smallest key in its right subtree), then delete the successor from the right subtree. The successor has no left child, so that second delete is always case 1 or 2.

```python
def delete(node, key):
    if node is None:
        return None
    if key < node.key:
        node.left = delete(node.left, key)
    elif key > node.key:
        # Reconnect the repaired right
        # subtree.
        node.right = delete(node.right, key)
    else:
        # cases 1 and 2: 0 or 1 child
        if node.left is None:
            return node.right
        if node.right is None:
            return node.left
        # case 3: two children
        succ = node.right
        while succ.left:
            succ = succ.left
        # Copy the next sorted key, then
        # remove it.
        node.key = succ.key
        # Reconnect the repaired right
        # subtree.
        node.right = delete(node.right,
                            succ.key)
    return node
```

Deleting 30 (two children) from the example: its successor is 35, the leftmost node in its right subtree. Copy 35 into 30's node, then delete the old 35 leaf.

```
 before            after
     30                35
    /  \              /  \
  20    40          20    40
       /  \                 \
     35    45                45
```

Why does the successor work? It is larger than everything in the left subtree (it came from the right) and smaller than everything else in the right subtree (it was the minimum there). The **in-order predecessor** (maximum of the left subtree) works equally well.

> [!warning] Copying keys is not always allowed
> Copying the successor's key into the node is fine for a textbook, but in real code other objects may hold references to nodes (iterators, handles). Production implementations such as the Linux rbtree and common C++ standard-library `std::map` implementations instead **relink** the successor node into the deleted node's position, so a node never changes key.

Always using the successor (known as **Hibbard deletion**) is asymmetric: right subtrees keep losing their minimum, and after long random sequences of inserts and deletes the tree becomes visibly skewed to the left, and searches can degrade relative to the insertion-only random-tree model. Choosing between successor and predecessor does not establish a logarithmic-height guarantee. A self-balancing policy does.

## Key takeaways
- Remove a leaf, splice a single child, or substitute a two-child node.
- The successor is the smallest key in the right subtree.
- Reconnect each returned subtree root after a recursive deletion.

## Further reading
- [Binary search tree — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_search_tree)
- [Binary Search Trees — Algorithms, 4th ed. (Sedgewick & Wayne)](https://algs4.cs.princeton.edu/32bst/)

lessons.title: Successors and global BST validation
lessons.summary: A successor is the next key in sorted order, not necessarily a child.
lessons.body:
Earlier units established a strict BST ordering with distinct, mutually comparable keys: every left-subtree key is smaller and every right-subtree key larger. Use the Node with key, left and right fields introduced in the search unit. Here n counts keys and h measures tree height in edges. Comparisons have constant cost; recursive code remains limited by Python call depth.

## In-order successor

"What is the next key after k?" comes up in ordered maps (`TreeMap.higherKey`), range scans and iterators. Two cases:

1. If the node has a **right subtree**, the successor is the **leftmost node** of that subtree. Successor of 30 is 35.
2. Otherwise, it is the nearest **ancestor whose left subtree contains the node**. Successor of 45 is 50: walking up, 45 is in 40's right, 40 is in 30's right, but 30 is in 50's left.

Without parent pointers you can find it top-down from the root: every time you go left, the current node is a candidate.

```python
def successor(root, key):
    succ, node = None, root
    while node:
        if key < node.key:
            # A left turn finds a greater
            # key.
            succ = node    # candidate
            node = node.left
        else:
            node = node.right
    return succ
```

This also works for keys that are not in the tree (successor of 47 is 50) and returns None for the maximum. It is O(h), where h is the tree's height: one step per level.

## Validating a BST

A classic interview question with a classic wrong answer: check that each node's left child is smaller and its right child is larger.

```
      10
     /  \
    5    15
        /
       6        <- 6 is below 10, yet is in
                   10's right subtree
```

Every parent-child pair here looks fine, but 6 sits in the right subtree of 10, so this is **not** a BST. The damage is real: searching for 6 goes left at 10 because 6 is smaller, then right at 5, and falls off the tree. The key is present but unreachable.

The fix is to pass down the range each node must fall within. This numeric example requires finite keys comparable with float infinities; it rejects NaN and infinite keys, and is not a validator for arbitrary string or custom-object keys:

```python
def is_bst(node, lo=float('-inf'),
           hi=float('inf')):
    if node is None:
        return True
    k = node.key
    # Ancestor bounds constrain the entire
    # path.
    if not (lo < k < hi):
        return False
    return (is_bst(node.left, lo, k) and
            is_bst(node.right, k, hi))
```

Going left tightens the upper bound; going right tightens the lower bound. An equivalent approach does an in-order traversal and checks each key is greater than the previous one. Both are O(n) for n nodes, since every node must be checked.

## Key takeaways
- A successor is the next key in sorted order, not necessarily a child.
- Ancestor bounds expose violations that local comparisons miss.
- Strict bounds match the distinct-key policy used here.

lessons.title: Insertion order, degeneration and rebuilding
lessons.summary: Sorted insertion creates a chain in an unbalanced BST.
lessons.body:
Earlier units established a strict BST ordering with distinct, mutually comparable keys: every left-subtree key is smaller and every right-subtree key larger. Use the Node with key, left and right fields introduced in the search unit. Here n counts keys and h measures tree height in edges. Comparisons have constant cost; recursive code remains limited by Python call depth.

## Degenerate trees

Search and single-key updates cost O(h + 1) for a tree of height h; full validation of n nodes costs O(n). With insertion only, order determines shape; deletions also change it.

| Input order | Shape | Height with 1,000 keys |
|---|---|---|
| Ascending | Right chain | 999 |
| Uniformly random permutation | Random shape | Expected O(log n); no fixed height |
| Median first, recursively | Shortest possible | 9 |

Inserting sorted keys into a plain BST produces a linked list with extra pointers. Each new key is larger than everything already stored, so it goes right at every node and walks the whole chain built so far: the first insert visits no existing nodes, the second visits 1, the third 2, and so on.

Adding those up gives about half the square of the number of keys, so the total work grows **quadratically**: ten times as many sorted keys costs about a hundred times as much. 1,000 sorted keys cost about half a million node visits; a million keys cost about 500 billion. Searches afterwards are no better: looking up a late key walks the chain like a linked-list scan.

Random insertion order is much kinder. For distinct keys inserted in a uniformly random permutation, the average depth of a stored key grows only logarithmically: for large trees it is about 1.39 times the depth of the best possible shape.

```formula reference
D ≈ 2 ln(n) ≈ 1.39 log_2(n)
where
D: the expected (average) depth, in edges, of a uniformly chosen key in a BST built from a random insertion order; this is the leading term only
n: the number of distinct keys in the tree
ln(n): the natural logarithm of n, about 0.693 times log_2(n)
log_2(n): the base-2 logarithm of n: how many times you can halve n before reaching 1
≈: approximately equal to
In words: for large trees, a randomly built BST is on average only about 39 % deeper than the best possible shape.
```

For 1,000 random keys the exact expected average depth is about 11, against about 8 in the best (complete) shape, whose height is 9. Expected height is also logarithmic, but this is an average over random orders, not a bound on every insertion order.

But real data is rarely random. Timestamps, auto-increment IDs and alphabetically sorted imports all arrive in order. For workloads requiring worst-case logarithmic access, use a **self-balancing** tree (AVL, red-black; the balanced-tree units), a B-tree (System Design, databases), a skip list, or a sorted sequence implementation. Python sortedcontainers uses a list of sorted lists; Redis can use a skip list plus dictionary or a compact encoding for sorted sets.

> [!tip] Building a balanced BST from sorted data
> If you have all the keys up front and sorted, pick the **middle** key as the root and recurse on each half. For a nonempty sorted set of distinct keys, passing index ranges rather than copying slices builds the shortest possible tree (height 3 for the ten keys above, 9 for 1,000 keys) in O(n) time, assuming constant-time node creation.

## Key takeaways
- Sorted insertion creates a chain in an unbalanced BST.
- Random insertion gives expected logarithmic depth, rather than a worst-case guarantee.
- A sorted batch can be built from midpoint index ranges without copying slices.

## Further reading
- [Binary Search Trees — Algorithms, 4th ed. (Sedgewick & Wayne)](https://algs4.cs.princeton.edu/32bst/)
- [Sorted Containers (Python) docs](https://grantjenks.com/docs/sortedcontainers/)

lessons.title: Rotations and the AVL balance rule
lessons.summary: A rotation preserves in-order order while changing local parent links.
lessons.body:
A plain BST is only as good as its insertion order. Feed it sorted keys and it becomes a linked list. AVL and red-black trees maintain balancing invariants after updates, using local rotations and metadata changes. Other balancing schemes can rebuild subtrees instead.

The result is a hard guarantee: for n keys, the height stays O(log n) (growing only with the logarithm of n, a small multiple of about 20 for a million keys) no matter what order keys arrive in, so search, insert and delete are **O(log n) worst case**. The two classic designs are **AVL trees** (1962) and **red-black trees** (1972 as symmetric B-trees; the red/black formulation dates from 1978). They differ in how strict their invariant is.

## Rotations

A rotation changes the shape of a small part of the tree while **preserving the in-order sequence**, so the BST property still holds.

```
      y                 x
     / \    right      / \
    x   C   ---->     A   y
   / \      <----        / \
  A   B     left        B   C
```

Here A, B and C are whole subtrees. In both shapes the in-order sequence is A, x, B, y, C. A right rotation at y lifts x up one level and pushes y down; subtree **B changes parent** from x to y. A left rotation is the mirror image.

A rotation updates a constant number of links and metadata fields and does no searching, so it is **O(1)**: a fixed amount of work, however big the tree. AVL and red-black trees use rotations plus bookkeeping (heights for AVL, colours for red-black).

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a group photo on tiered steps
> A group stands on tiered steps for a photo, arranged left to right in name order. The photographer asks one person to step up a tier and their neighbour to step down. Heights in the picture change, but reading the faces from left to right still gives the same alphabetical order.
>
> **How it maps:** left-to-right order is the in-order sequence, which a rotation never changes. The tier each person stands on is their depth: a right rotation lifts x up a level and drops y down one, which is how rotations shorten a tall side.
>
> **Where it stops:** people in a photo have no parent links. In a tree, the middle subtree B must be handed from x to y so that every node still has exactly one parent; forgetting that hand-over is the classic rotation bug.

```python
def rotate_right(y):
    x = y.left
    # Transfer the middle subtree
    # before lifting.
    y.left = x.right           # move B
    x.right = y
    # Fix the lowered node before its
    # new parent.
    fix(y)                     # update
    fix(x)                     # heights
    return x                   # new root
```

## AVL trees

Named after Adelson-Velsky and Landis, the AVL tree was the first self-balancing BST.

**Invariant:** at every node, the heights of the left and right subtrees differ by at most 1. The difference is the node's **balance factor**:

```formula essential
b(x) = h(x_L) − h(x_R)
b(x) ∈ {−1, 0, +1}
where
b(x): the balance factor of node x; positive means left-heavy, negative means right-heavy
x: any node in the tree
h(x_L): the height of x's left subtree, in edges; −1 if the subtree is empty
h(x_R): the height of x's right subtree, in edges; −1 if the subtree is empty
∈: "is one of": the value must be in the set that follows
{ }: a set of allowed values
In words: a node's balance factor is its left subtree's height minus its right subtree's height, and an AVL tree requires it to be −1, 0 or +1 at every node.
```

The sign tells you which side is too tall: +2 means the left side is two levels taller, −2 the right. For example, if node 30's left child 10 has a child of its own (left height 1) and 30 has no right child (height −1), its balance factor is 2, which breaks the invariant. The later insertion unit's `bf(n)` computes exactly this, and the sign decides which rotation repairs it.

## Key takeaways
- A rotation preserves in-order order while changing local parent links.
- The middle subtree changes parent during a rotation.
- AVL balance factors compare left and right subtree heights.

## Further reading
- [AVL tree — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AVL_tree)
- [AVL tree visualisation — USF](https://www.cs.usfca.edu/~galles/visualization/AVLtree.html)
