lessons.title: Minimum AVL nodes and the height bound
lessons.summary: The sparsest allowed children differ in height by one.
lessons.body:
Start with the distinct-key BST ordering from the previous units. A rotation must keep the same sorted in-order sequence while changing local links. Here n counts stored keys and h measures real-node height in edges; empty subtrees have height minus one unless a NIL-path convention is explicitly given. Height bounds assume constant-cost key comparisons, rather than measuring application latency.

## Why the AVL rule guarantees O(log n)

The AVL rule only says each node's two subtree heights may differ by one. Why does such a local rule stop the whole tree growing tall? Turn the question round: what is the **fewest** nodes an AVL tree of a given height can have?

The sparsest AVL tree of height h is as lopsided as the rule allows at every node: a root, one subtree of height h − 1 and the other of height h − 2, each of those as sparse as possible in turn. So the minimum node count for each height is the previous two minimums added together, plus one for the root:

| Height (edges) | Fewest nodes |
|---|---|
| 0 | 1 |
| 1 | 2 |
| 2 | 4 |
| 3 | 7 |
| 4 | 12 |
| 5 | 20 |
| 6 | 33 |

Adding the previous two terms is how Fibonacci numbers grow, and indeed each count is one less than a Fibonacci number. Fibonacci numbers grow by about 1.618 times per step, so even the sparsest AVL tree needs **exponentially** more nodes for every extra level. Turned round, the height can only grow logarithmically with the node count:

```formula reference
N(h) = N(h − 1) + N(h − 2) + 1
h_max ≈ 1.44 log_2(n)
where
h: the height of the AVL tree, in edges
N(h): the smallest number of nodes an AVL tree of height h can have; N(0) = 1 and N(1) = 2
h_max: the greatest height an AVL tree with n nodes can have, for large n
n: the number of nodes (keys) in the tree
log_2(n): the base-2 logarithm of n: how many times you can halve n before reaching 1
≈: approximately equal to (a leading-term approximation for large n)
In words: the sparsest AVL tree of each height is a root over the two previous sparsest trees, so node counts grow like Fibonacci numbers and the worst-case height is about 1.44 times the best possible.
```

For a million keys, the exact minimum counts show an AVL tree can have height at most 27 edges (height 28 would need 1,346,268 nodes), against 19 for a complete tree. That is the hard guarantee: whatever order a million keys arrive in, a search visits at most 28 nodes, and inserts and deletes repair along a path no longer than that.

The 1.44 factor is a large-tree approximation; for an exact finite limit, use the minimum counts, as above.

## Key takeaways
- The sparsest allowed children differ in height by one.
- Minimum node counts obey a Fibonacci-related recurrence.
- Use exact counts when deciding a finite maximum height.

## Further reading
- [AVL tree — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AVL_tree)
- [AVL tree visualisation — USF](https://www.cs.usfca.edu/~galles/visualization/AVLtree.html)

options.text: Nothing: AVL trees only promise logarithmic height on average, not in the worst case
options.explanation: AVL height is a worst-case guarantee. The rule holds after every insert and delete, whatever order keys arrive in.

options.text: The rule holds at every node, so even the sparsest AVL tree needs Fibonacci-like, exponentially growing node counts per level; a million keys allow a height of at most 27
options.explanation: Correct. The sparsest tree of each height is a root over the two previous sparsest trees, so node counts grow about 1.6 times per level. A million keys cannot reach a height above 27 under that rule.

options.text: AVL trees periodically rebuild themselves into perfect trees, which resets the height
options.explanation: AVL trees never rebuild wholesale. They repair locally with rotations on the path that changed, and the invariant alone bounds the height.

options.text: The rule is only checked at the root, but rotations happen to keep the rest of the tree short
options.explanation: The rule is checked at every node on the update path, and must hold at every node. A rule enforced only at the root would allow both subtrees to be long chains.

questions.workedExample:
1. Ask the opposite question: what is the fewest nodes an AVL tree of height h can contain?
2. To be as sparse as possible, the root has one subtree of height h − 1 and one of height h − 2, each itself as sparse as possible. So the minimum count for each height is the previous two minimums plus one: 1, 2, 4, 7, 12, 20, 33 …
3. That is Fibonacci-style growth, about 1.6 times more nodes per extra level. Exponential growth in nodes means the height can only grow logarithmically.
4. Working through the exact counts, height 27 needs 832,039 nodes and height 28 needs 1,346,268. A million keys therefore allow a height of at most 27 edges, compared with 19 for a complete tree.

The colleague's mistake is treating the rule as local slack that can accumulate. Because it applies at every node, the slack cannot pile up into a long chain.

lessons.title: AVL insertion and single or double repair
lessons.summary: Repair LL and RR cases with a single rotation.
lessons.body:
Start with the distinct-key BST ordering from the previous units. A rotation must keep the same sorted in-order sequence while changing local links. Here n counts stored keys and h measures real-node height in edges; empty subtrees have height minus one unless a NIL-path convention is explicitly given. Height bounds assume constant-cost key comparisons, rather than measuring application latency.

## Insert and rebalance

Insert as in a plain BST, then walk back up the path updating heights. At the first node whose balance factor becomes +2 or −2, one of four cases applies, named after the path from that node down to where the new key went.

| Case | Shape | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| LL | left child left-heavy | rotate right |
| RR | right child right-heavy | rotate left |
| LR | left child right-heavy | left at child, then right |
| RL | right child left-heavy | right at child, then left |

The LR case is the one people miss. Insert 30, 10, 20:

```
  30           30           20
  /            /           /  \
10    -->    20    -->   10    30
  \          /
   20      10
 (LR)   rotate left   rotate right
        at 10         at 30
```

A single right rotation at 30 would just move the zig-zag to the other side; you have to straighten it first.

The insertion function below uses rotate_right from the rotation unit; the Node, height helpers and rotate_left needed to run it are provided just after it. Together those definitions form the complete distinct-key insertion example.

```python
def insert(n, key):
    if n is None:
        return Node(key)
    if key < n.key:
        n.left = insert(n.left, key)
    elif key > n.key:
        n.right = insert(n.right, key)
    else:
        return n
    # Child updates change the cached
    # height.
    fix(n)                     # height
    b = bf(n)
    if b > 1:                  # left-heavy
        if bf(n.left) < 0:     # LR case
            n.left = rotate_left(n.left)
        return rotate_right(n)
    if b < -1:                 # right-heavy
        if bf(n.right) > 0:    # RL case
            n.right = rotate_right(n.right)
        return rotate_left(n)
    return n
```

The following helpers complete the example. Keys are distinct comparable values; duplicate insertions leave the tree unchanged.

```python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, key):
        self.key = key
        self.left = self.right = None
        self.height = 0

def ht(n):
    return -1 if n is None else n.height

def fix(n):
    n.height = 1 + max(ht(n.left),
                       ht(n.right))

def bf(n):
    return ht(n.left) - ht(n.right)

def rotate_left(x):
    y = x.right
    # Transfer the middle subtree
    # symmetrically.
    x.right = y.left
    y.left = x
    fix(x)
    fix(y)
    return y
```

Inserting 1 to 7 in order into this AVL tree gives the perfect tree with 4 at the root, where a plain BST would give a chain.

After an insert that creates imbalance, one rebalancing step (one single or one double rotation) restores balance, because it returns the subtree to the height it had before the insert, so no ancestor needs fixing. Deletion is worse: a rotation can shrink a subtree's height, unbalancing its parent in turn, so a delete in a tree of n keys may need **O(log n) rotations**, up to one per level of the path.

## Key takeaways
- Repair LL and RR cases with a single rotation.
- Straighten a zig-zag before the second rotation in LR and RL cases.
- Insert and delete differ in whether height changes propagate.

## Further reading
- [AVL tree — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AVL_tree)
- [AVL tree visualisation — USF](https://www.cs.usfca.edu/~galles/visualization/AVLtree.html)

questions.prompt: You insert 10, then 20, then 30 into an empty **AVL tree**. What does the tree look like afterwards?

options.text: A chain 10 → 20 → 30 going right
options.explanation: That is a plain BST. After 30 is inserted, 10 has balance factor −2 and the AVL tree must rotate.

options.text: 20 at the root with children 10 and 30
options.explanation: Correct. The RR case at 10 is fixed by a single left rotation, lifting 20 to the root.

options.text: 10 at the root with 30 as right child and 20 as its left child
options.explanation: This is a valid BST ordering, but it is not AVL-balanced: root 10 has an empty left subtree and a right subtree of height 1.

options.text: 30 at the root with children 10 and 20
options.explanation: With 10 as the left child and 20 as the right child of 30, the right-child key is too small. The AVL rotation instead promotes 20.

questions.workedExample:
1. Insert 10: root.
2. Insert 20: right child of 10. The balance factor at node 10 is minus one (allowed).
3. Insert 30: right child of 20. Now 10's left side is empty (height −1) and its right subtree, 20 → 30, has height 1. Node 10's balance factor (left height minus right height) is −1 − 1 = −2: its right side is two levels taller, which the AVL rule forbids.
4. The path from 10 is right, right: the **RR case**. Fix with one left rotation at 10.

```
10                 20
  \               /  \
   20     -->    10    30
     \
      30
```

questions.prompt:
Using the lesson's AVL `insert`, you add **33** to this AVL tree. After rebalancing, what is the root of 50's left subtree?

```
          50
        /    \
      30      70
     /  \    /  \
   20   40  60   80
       /  \
      35  45
```

options.text: 30, because no rotation is needed
options.explanation: After inserting 33 under 35, node 30 has a left height of 0 and a right height of 2: balance factor −2, so it must be rebalanced.

options.text: 40, after a single left rotation at 30
options.explanation: The new key went right then *left* from 30 (into 40's left subtree). That is the RL case; a single left rotation leaves a zig-zag and 40's subtree is still unbalanced.

options.text: 33, because the new key is always moved to the top
options.explanation: AVL rotations lift the middle key of the unbalanced triple, not the newly inserted one.

options.text: 35, after a right rotation at 40 then a left rotation at 30
options.explanation: Correct. This is the RL case: straighten the zig-zag by rotating right at 40, then rotate left at 30. 35 rises to the top with children 30 and 40.

questions.workedExample:
1. BST insert: 33 < 50, > 30, < 40, < 35, so 33 becomes 35's left child.
2. Walk back up updating heights: 35 now has height 1, 40 has height 2, and 30 has a left subtree (20) of height 0 and a right subtree (40) of height 2. So 30's balance factor (left height minus right height) is 0 − 2 = −2: it is two levels heavier on the right. Its right child 40 has balance factor 1 − 0 = +1: it leans left.
3. 30 is the first unbalanced node, and its right child is left-heavy: the **RL** case.
4. Rotate right at 40, then left at 30:

```
       35
     /    \
   30      40
  /  \       \
 20   33     45
```

Every balance factor is now in {−1, 0, +1}, and in-order is 20 30 33 35 40 45.

questions.prompt: Why does an AVL **insert** need at most one rebalancing step (one single or one double rotation), while an AVL **delete** may need a rotation at every level up to the root?

options.text: After an insert, the rotation restores the subtree to its height before the insert, so no ancestor's balance changes; after a delete, a rotation can leave the subtree one level shorter, unbalancing the parent
options.explanation: Correct. Insert-rebalancing undoes the height increase completely. Delete has already shrunk the subtree, and the rotation can shrink it again, so the imbalance can propagate upward.

options.text: Deletes must rebuild the subtree from scratch
options.explanation: No rebuild is needed; deletes use the same O(1) rotations, just possibly more of them.

options.text: Inserts only touch leaves while deletes touch internal nodes
options.explanation: Both operations start at the bottom (a delete always ends up removing a node with at most one child) and walk up the same path.

options.text: Deletes need to check every node in the tree
options.explanation: Only the nodes on the path from the removed node back to the root can have changed height, so only those are checked.

questions.workedExample:
1. Insert: a child subtree grew by one level, making its parent unbalanced.
2. The (single or double) rotation at that parent returns the repaired subtree to the height it had **before** the insert. Ancestors see no change, so the fix-up stops.
3. Delete: some subtree shrank by one, making its parent unbalanced. Repair fixes that parent, but the resulting subtree may have height one less than before. Now the next ancestor may be unbalanced, and so on.
4. Worst case: one single or double rebalancing step per level, O(log n) rotations for n keys. This is one reason libraries favour red-black trees, which need at most 3 rotations per delete.

lessons.title: Red-black paths and height
lessons.summary: NIL child positions count as black for the path invariant.
lessons.body:
Start with the distinct-key BST ordering from the previous units. A rotation must keep the same sorted in-order sequence while changing local links. Here n counts stored keys and h measures real-node height in edges; empty subtrees have height minus one unless a NIL-path convention is explicitly given. Height bounds assume constant-cost key comparisons, rather than measuring application latency.

## Red-black trees

A red-black tree relaxes the invariant. Instead of near-perfect balance, it only promises that root-to-NIL paths differ in length by at most a factor of two. In exchange, it does less restructuring.

Every node is coloured red or black, and empty (NIL) children count as black leaves. The rules:

1. The root is black.
2. A red node has no red children (no two reds in a row).
3. Every path from a node down to a NIL leaf passes through the **same number of black nodes**: its **black-height**.

```
          13B
        /     \
      8R       17R
     /  \     /   \
   1B   11B 15B   25B
     \           /
      6R       22R
```

Every root-to-NIL path here has 3 black nodes, counting the root and the NIL itself (for example 13, 8, 1, 6, NIL passes 13, 1 and NIL), and no red node has a red child.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: checkpoints on routes out of a city
> Every route from a city's centre to its edge must pass the same number of official checkpoints. Between checkpoints a route may have at most one optional rest stop, never two in a row. However the roads are laid out, no route to the edge can have more than about twice as many stops as the route with the fewest.
>
> **How it maps:** routes are root-to-NIL paths, checkpoints are black nodes, and the equal checkpoint count is the black-height rule. Rest stops are red nodes, and "never two in a row" is the no-red-red rule. Together they cap how many more nodes one path can have than another.
>
> **Where it stops:** roads do not change. A red-black tree must recolour and rotate after every insert or delete to keep both rules true, and the rules bound only the *ratio* of path lengths; the logarithmic height comes from also counting how many nodes the checkpoints force into the tree.

### Why the height is O(log n)

Two facts combine:

- **Paths are within a factor of two.** No two reds are adjacent, so at least half the nodes on any root-to-NIL path are black. Every path has the same number of black nodes, so the longest root-to-NIL path is at most twice as long as the shortest.
- **Black nodes force lots of nodes.** Ignoring the red nodes, every path down from the root meets the same number of black nodes, so the black nodes alone behave like a perfectly balanced tree. If every path from a node down to NIL meets b black nodes (counting the NIL but not the node itself), that node's subtree must contain at least 2 to the power b, minus 1, real nodes; this can be proved by induction.

Put together, the black levels can only be about log₂ n deep, and the full height at most twice that:

```formula reference
h ≤ 2 log_2(n + 1)
where
h: the height of the tree, in edges
n: the number of keys (real, non-NIL nodes) in the tree
log_2(n + 1): the base-2 logarithm of n + 1: how many times you can halve n + 1 before reaching 1
≤: is at most
In words: a red-black tree is never more than about twice as tall as the shortest possible binary tree with the same number of keys.
```

For a million keys the bound is a height of about 40 edges, against 19 for a complete tree and at most 27 for an AVL tree. That looser bound is the price of red-black trees' cheaper repairs. Actual height depends on the implementation and update history.

Java TreeMap uses this red-black structure. Its documented logarithmic get, put and remove guarantees hold for insertion orders such as ascending IDs; ordered arrivals do not turn it into the unbalanced chain studied earlier.

## Key takeaways
- NIL child positions count as black for the path invariant.
- No consecutive red nodes and equal black-height imply logarithmic height.
- Red-black height is bounded by about twice the best possible; AVL is stricter but may rotate more on deletes.

## Further reading
- [Red–black tree — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red%E2%80%93black_tree)
- [Balanced Search Trees — Algorithms, 4th ed. (Sedgewick & Wayne)](https://algs4.cs.princeton.edu/33balanced/)
- [TreeMap (Java SE 25) — Oracle](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/util/TreeMap.html)

questions.prompt: A service loads one million order IDs into a Java `TreeMap` in ascending order. Roughly how many nodes, at most, does a later `get` examine?

options.text: About 1,000,000, because sorted input makes the tree a chain
options.explanation: That is a plain BST. TreeMap is a red-black tree, which rebalances on every insert, so sorted input cannot build a chain.

options.text: Exactly 1, because TreeMap hashes keys
options.explanation: That is HashMap. TreeMap keeps keys ordered and searches by comparison.

options.text: About 1,000 (square-root growth)
options.explanation: The square root of the key count is 1,000 here. Its red-black height guarantee is logarithmic rather than square-root growth; the red-black rules force logarithmic height.

options.text: At most about 40
options.explanation: Correct. A red-black tree's height is at most twice the base-2 logarithm of one more than the key count, a height of about 40 edges for a million keys, regardless of insertion order.

questions.workedExample:
1. TreeMap is a red-black tree.
2. Its rules cap the height at about twice the base-2 logarithm of the key count: a height of about 40 edges for a million keys, whatever order the keys arrived in. Ascending input triggers rotations and recolourings during the load, but never builds a chain.
3. So a get examines at most about 41 nodes (one per level on the path, including the root).
4. Actual search length depends on the resulting tree; the height bound alone does not establish a 20–25-node typical path.
5. A plain BST with the same input would be a chain of a million nodes: a lookup for the largest ID would walk all of them.

questions.prompt: Which statements are true of **every** valid red-black tree? Select all that apply.

options.text: No root-to-NIL path is more than twice as long as any other
options.explanation: Correct. all paths below the root have the same black count, including NIL. Because reds cannot be adjacent, such path lengths lie between that black count and twice it.

options.text: Every red node's children are black
options.explanation: Correct. That is the 'no two reds in a row' rule (NIL children count as black).

options.text: All leaves are at the same depth
options.explanation: Only the black nodes are evenly spread. Red nodes stretch some paths, so leaf depths can differ (by up to a factor of two).

options.text: Every path from a given node down to a NIL leaf has the same number of black nodes
options.explanation: Correct. This is the black-height rule; it holds at every node, not just the root.

options.text: Every node's balance factor is in {−1, 0, +1}
options.explanation: That is the AVL invariant. A red-black tree can have subtrees whose heights differ by more than one.

questions.workedExample:
1. Rules 2 and 3 together give the factor-of-two bound. True.
2. Rule 2 directly. True.
3. Depths vary: in the lesson's example, leaf 11 has depth 2 and leaf 6 has depth 3. False.
4. Rule 3 directly. True.
5. Counter-example (a valid red-black tree; every root-to-NIL path has 3 black nodes counting NIL):

```
     B
    / \
   B   R
      / \
     B   B
    / \
   R   R
```

The root's left subtree has height 0 and its right subtree height 2: balance factor −2, illegal in an AVL tree. False.

questions.prompt: You are choosing an ordered-map structure for about a million keys and want a worst-case bound on search path length. Which comparison of worst-case heights is right?

options.text: Red-black trees are stricter than AVL trees, so their worst-case height is lower
options.explanation: It is the other way round. AVL's rule (subtree heights differ by at most one at every node) is stricter than red-black's factor-of-two path rule, so AVL's worst case is lower.

options.text: Red-black trees only bound colours, not heights, so their worst case is a chain like a plain BST
options.explanation: The colour rules do bound height: equal black counts on every path plus no red-red pairs force the height to be at most about twice the base-2 logarithm of the key count.

options.text: Both are logarithmic, but red-black's worst case is looser: height about 40 against at most 27 for AVL, and 19 for a complete tree
options.explanation: Correct. Red-black allows paths up to twice the shortest, giving a bound of about 40 for a million keys; AVL's Fibonacci-style minimum sizes cap it at 27. Both are tiny compared with a plain BST's possible chain of nearly a million.

options.text: Both guarantee a complete tree, so both have height at most 19
options.explanation: Neither keeps the tree complete. Both allow some imbalance in exchange for cheap local repairs, so their worst cases are taller than the complete tree's 19.

questions.workedExample:
1. A complete tree of a million keys has height 19: the best any binary tree can do.
2. AVL: every node's two subtree heights differ by at most one. The sparsest trees grow like Fibonacci numbers, which caps a million-key AVL tree at height 27.
3. Red-black: no two reds in a row and the same number of blacks on every path, so the longest root-to-NIL path is at most twice as long as the shortest. That gives a bound of about twice the base-2 logarithm, a height of about 40 for a million keys.
4. Both bounds are logarithmic and hold for any insertion order. The trade-off is that red-black trees accept a looser shape in exchange for less restructuring, which is one reason standard libraries such as Java's TreeMap use them.

| Tree | Worst-case height, about a million keys |
|---|---|
| Complete | 19 |
| AVL | 27 |
| Red-black | about 40 |
| Plain BST | nearly a million |

These are bounds on the shape, not measured lookup times.

lessons.title: Red-black insertion and colour repair
lessons.summary: Repair insertion colours with uncle cases and rotations.
lessons.body:
The preceding unit defined red-black invariants: a black root, no red parent with a red child, and equal black-height on every path to a NIL child. Start with strict BST ordering and distinct comparable keys. Here n counts stored keys. This is the conventional bottom-up repair outline, rather than an executable insertion implementation; left-leaning and other variants have different repair rules.

## Insertion and colour repair

1. Insert as in a BST and colour the new node **red** (this preserves rule 3; rule 2 or the root-colour rule may need repair).
2. If its parent is black, done.
3. If its parent is red, look at the **uncle** (the parent's sibling):
   - **Uncle red:** recolour parent and uncle black and the grandparent red, then repeat the check from the grandparent. No rotation; the problem moves up two levels.
   - **Uncle black:** one or two rotations around the grandparent plus a recolour fix it for good.
4. Colour the root black.

For the conventional bottom-up red-black algorithms, insertion uses at most two rotations and deletion at most three. Recolouring and fix-up traversal can take O(log n) steps in one update of a tree of n keys, because the red-uncle case can repeat up the whole path. These rotation bounds do not apply automatically to every red-black variant.

> [!note] Red-black trees are 2-3-4 trees in disguise
> Glue each black node to its red children and you get a B-tree node with 2, 3 or 4 children. Rule 3 says all leaves of that B-tree are at the same depth. Sedgewick's **left-leaning red-black tree** (2008) restricts red links further and its 2-3 variant maps onto 2-3 trees, which makes the code much shorter.

## Key takeaways
- New nodes start red so existing black counts are unchanged.
- A red uncle allows recolouring and moves the conflict upward.
- A black uncle requires rotations and recolouring; restore the root to black.

## Further reading
- [Red–black tree — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red%E2%80%93black_tree)
- [Left-leaning Red-Black Trees — Robert Sedgewick (PDF)](https://sedgewick.io/wp-content/themes/sedgewick/papers/2008LLRB.pdf)
- [Red-black Trees (rbtree) in Linux — kernel docs](https://docs.kernel.org/core-api/rbtree.html)

questions.prompt: In a red-black tree you insert a new node (coloured red). Its **parent is red** and its **uncle is red**. What does the fix-up do?

options.text: Rotate at the grandparent and swap colours, then stop
options.explanation: That is the black-uncle case. With a red uncle, rotating is unnecessary: recolouring alone restores black-height.

options.text: Recolour the new node black and stop
options.explanation: Making the new node black adds one black node to some paths but not others, breaking the equal black-height rule.

options.text: Delete and re-insert the parent
options.explanation: Red-black trees never re-insert nodes; fix-ups are local recolourings and rotations.

options.text: Recolour parent and uncle black and the grandparent red, then repeat the check at the grandparent
options.explanation: Correct. Black-height is unchanged through the grandparent, but the grandparent may now be red under a red parent, so the check moves two levels up.

questions.workedExample:
1. Red parent + red new node violates 'no red-red'.
2. The grandparent must be black (the tree was valid before).
3. Push the grandparent's blackness down: parent and uncle become black, grandparent becomes red. Every path through the grandparent still has the same number of black nodes.
4. The grandparent might now have a red parent, so repeat from there. If it reaches the root, colour the root black.

This case does no rotations; at most 2 rotations happen in total, in the black-uncle case that ends the fix-up.

lessons.title: Choosing balanced trees for real workloads
lessons.summary: AVL has a tighter worst-case height bound, but speed needs measurement.
lessons.body:
Start with the distinct-key BST ordering from the previous units. A rotation must keep the same sorted in-order sequence while changing local links. Here n counts stored keys and h measures real-node height in edges; empty subtrees have height minus one unless a NIL-path convention is explicitly given. Height bounds assume constant-cost key comparisons, rather than measuring application latency.

## AVL versus red-black

The previous units gave each tree's worst-case height. For a million keys, an AVL tree has height at most 27 edges and a red-black tree at most about 40, against 19 for a complete tree. Both are logarithmic in the number of keys n; the difference is a constant factor, traded against how much repair work each update does.

| | AVL | Red-black |
|---|---|---|
| Max height | Approx. 1.44 times the base-2 logarithm | Twice the base-2 log of the key count plus one |
| Lookup height bound | Tighter | Looser |
| Rotations/insert | One single or double rotation | At most two |
| Rotations/delete | O(log n) | At most three |
| Extra data | Height or balance factor | 1 colour bit |

Search and single-key updates are O(log n) for n keys, with constant-cost comparisons; traversing all entries is O(n). Practical tradeoffs:

- AVL offers a tighter worst-case height bound; actual read performance needs measurement.
- **Write-heavy** or general-purpose libraries usually choose red-black: fewer rotations on delete, and a colour bit can be hidden in the low bit of an aligned pointer, as the Linux kernel does.

## Where they are used

- **Java `TreeMap` and `TreeSet`**: red-black trees, giving logarithmic get, put, floorKey and ceilingKey operations; full sorted iteration over n entries takes O(n).
- **Java `HashMap`**: since Java 8, when a single bucket grows past 8 colliding entries (in a table of at least 64 buckets), it is converted into a small red-black tree. Comparable keys can use ordering to obtain logarithmic bin searches. Equal-hash keys without usable comparison ordering can still require linear search within a tree bin.
- **C++ `std::map` and `std::set`**: red-black trees in the major standard libraries (libstdc++, libc++, MSVC). The standard requires logarithmic key lookup and key-based updates for n elements, with other operation-specific bounds; erasing through a known iterator is amortised constant time. Insertion preserves iterators, without requiring a specific representation.
- **Linux kernel**: a generic intrusive rbtree (`lib/rbtree.c`) used widely. The **Completely Fair Scheduler** kept runnable tasks in a red-black tree ordered by `vruntime` (virtual runtime) and ran the leftmost task, caching a pointer to it so picking the next task is O(1). Linux began transitioning fair scheduling toward EEVDF in version 6.6; its implementation uses an augmented red-black tree. `epoll` also stores its watched file descriptors in one.

> [!example] Why CFS wanted a tree, not a binary heap
> A binary heap gives the minimum just as fast. But the scheduler also removes arbitrary tasks (one blocks on I/O, one is killed) and re-inserts them with new keys. With an intrusive tree, each task embeds its own tree node, so removing a given task from n runnable tasks is O(log n) with no search. A binary heap would need an extra position index to find an arbitrary entry, and it cannot cheaply answer "which task comes next after this one?".

### Other balanced structures, briefly

- **B-trees and B+ trees** use the same idea with hundreds of keys per node, matching disk pages. Many relational database indexes use them; hash, bitmap and other index types also exist (covered in System Design: databases).
- **Skip lists** give expected O(log n) search over n keys with randomised towers of linked lists; Redis sorted sets can use a skip list plus dictionary or a compact encoding.
- **Treaps** and **splay trees** balance with randomness or by moving accessed nodes to the root.
- Python has no built-in balanced tree. `sortedcontainers` uses a list of sorted lists, which offers different locality and update tradeoffs from pointer-based trees.

Which of these is fastest for a given program depends on the implementation, the key types, the hardware and the mix of reads and writes. Height bounds tell you what cannot go wrong; only a benchmark of your own workload tells you which is quicker.

## Key takeaways
- AVL has a tighter worst-case height bound, but speed needs measurement.
- Conventional red-black deletion uses a bounded number of rotations.
- Library and kernel uses must be distinguished from interface requirements.

## Further reading
- [Left-leaning Red-Black Trees — Robert Sedgewick (PDF)](https://sedgewick.io/wp-content/themes/sedgewick/papers/2008LLRB.pdf)

You must choose between an AVL tree and a red-black tree. Which has the tighter worst-case lookup-height bound, making it a candidate to benchmark for this workload?

options.text: Red-black, because it has a lower height bound
options.explanation: Backwards: red-black's worst-case height (about twice the base-2 logarithm of n) is looser than AVL's (about 1.44 times it).

options.text: AVL, because it has a tighter worst-case height bound
options.explanation: Correct. AVL has the tighter worst-case height bound. Actual latency and average path length still depend on the implementation, key distribution and hardware.

options.text: Red-black, because it does fewer rotations on lookups
options.explanation: Lookups never rotate in either tree. Rotations happen only on insert and delete.

options.text: It doesn't matter; both are O(log n)
options.explanation: Asymptotically equal, but with billions of lookups a constant-factor difference in depth adds up. The question is which constant to pay.

questions.workedExample:
1. Both trees give O(log n) search and single-key updates, so look at constants.
2. Lookup cost grows with the length of the search path, so compare the worst-case height bounds: about 1.44 times the base-2 logarithm of n for AVL, against about twice it for red-black. For a million keys that is a height of at most 27 edges against about 40. These are worst-case bounds, not measured averages.
3. Write cost: red-black does fewer rotations (at most two per insert and three per delete; AVL deletes can rotate O(log n) times). That matters for write-heavy work, but this workload barely writes.
4. So AVL is a candidate to benchmark for this read-dominated index, rather than a guaranteed runtime winner. (A sorted array with binary search would be simpler still if it is rebuilt nightly.)

questions.prompt: Which of these statements about real systems are true? Select all that apply.

options.explanation: Correct. Its Javadoc says so, and that is why `get`, `put` and `remove` are guaranteed O(log n) for n entries.

options.explanation: Correct. Once a bucket grows past 8 entries (and the table has at least 64 buckets), it is treeified, allowing logarithmic bin search when key ordering can distinguish collisions; non-comparable equal-hash keys can still require linear search.

lessons.title: Heap order and implicit array layout
lessons.summary: A binary heap combines complete shape with parent-child priority order.
lessons.body:
Many problems only ever need the **smallest** (or largest) item: the next job to run, the nearest unvisited city in Dijkstra's algorithm, the earliest timer to fire, the next event in a simulation. A BST can do that, but it keeps far more order than you need.

A **priority queue** is the abstract data type for this job: `push(item)`, `pop_min()` and `peek()`. The standard implementation is the **binary heap**. For a binary heap of n items it gives O(log n) push and pop (work growing with the logarithm of n, about 20 steps for a million items) and O(1) peek (a fixed cost), stored with implicit parent/child indices rather than tree-link pointers. Python lists still store references to their elements. Costs assume constant-time comparisons; dynamic-array resizing makes push/pop bounds amortized when allocation costs are included.

## The binary heap property

A binary **min-heap** is a binary tree with two rules:

1. **Shape:** it is a **complete binary tree** (every level full except possibly the last, which fills from the left).
2. **Order:** every parent is **less than or equal to** its children.

So the minimum is always at the root. A **max-heap** flips the order rule.

```
          1
        /   \
       3     2
      / \   / \
     4   8 7   6
    /
   9
```

Notice how much weaker this is than a BST. Siblings are unordered (3 is left of 2), and 4 sits deep on the left while 2 is near the top on the right. The binary heap only promises that every path from the root downward is sorted. That weaker promise is what makes it cheap to maintain.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a chain of command
> In a strict chain of command, every officer outranks the people directly under them, so the most senior person is always at the top. But two officers in different units are never compared, and someone low down in one unit may hold a higher rank than someone near the top of another.
>
> **How it maps:** "outranks" is the heap order (for a min-heap, "smaller key ranks higher"), the top officer is the root and the minimum, and units are subtrees. Only each chain from the top downwards is ordered; siblings and cousins are not.
>
> **Where it stops:** a real chain of command rarely changes shape. A heap reshuffles on every push and pop, and it must always stay a complete tree, filling each level from the left.

## The array layout

Because the tree is complete, it packs into an array in level order with no gaps (the tree-structure units):

```
idx:  0  1  2  3  4  5  6  7
val: [1, 3, 2, 4, 8, 7, 6, 9]
```

The parent and children of any slot are found by arithmetic on its index:

```formula essential
i_parent = ⌊(i − 1) / 2⌋
i_left = 2i + 1
i_right = 2i + 2
where
i: the index (0-based position) of an item in the array; i_parent applies only when i > 0
i_parent: the index of that item's parent
i_left: the index of its left child, if that index is less than the heap size
i_right: the index of its right child, if that index is less than the heap size
⌊ ⌋: floor: round down to a whole number, so ⌊2.5⌋ = 2
In words: the children of slot i are at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, and the parent is at (i − 1) halved and rounded down.
```

So the 3 at index 1 has children at indices 3 and 4 (4 and 8), and the 9 at index 7 has its parent at index 3 (the 4). In the Python code below, the parent index is `(i - 1) // 2`, where `//` divides and rounds down.

Avoiding explicit tree links saves their storage. The array of slots is contiguous, though referenced payload objects need not be; actual cache behaviour depends on layout and access patterns.

The second half of the array, rounded up, is all **leaves**. A slot has a child only if its left-child index is still inside the array, and that stops being true halfway along. In the 8-item example, indices 4 to 7 (values 8, 7, 6 and 9) are leaves: index 4's left child would be at 9, past the end. This fact matters later: building a heap only needs to repair the first half of the array, and with distinct keys the largest key in a min-heap must be somewhere in the leaf half.

```formula reference
⌊n / 2⌋ ≤ i ≤ n − 1
where
n: the number of items in the heap (at least 1)
i: the index of a leaf; every index in this range is a leaf, and no other index is
⌊ ⌋: floor: round down to a whole number
≤: is at most
In words: in an array heap, the leaves start halfway along (rounded down) and run to the end.
```

## Key takeaways
- A binary heap combines complete shape with parent-child priority order.
- Array indices replace explicit links.
- Binary heap order does not sort siblings or the entire array.

## Further reading
- [Binary heap — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_heap)
- [Priority Queues — Algorithms, 4th ed. (Sedgewick & Wayne)](https://algs4.cs.princeton.edu/24pq/)

questions.prompt: A colleague writes a 0-indexed array heap (root at index 0) but uses the textbook child positions `2*i` and `2*i + 1`, and parent `i // 2`. Pushes and pops start producing a corrupted heap. What is the underlying mistake?

options.text: Those formulas are for a 1-indexed layout; with the root at 0, the root's left child comes out as index 0, the root itself
options.explanation: Correct. With the root at index 0, 2 × 0 is 0, so the root becomes its own child and index 1 is treated as its only other child. Every later parent-child link is shifted too. A 0-indexed heap needs 2i + 1, 2i + 2 and (i − 1) // 2.

options.text: Heaps cannot be stored in arrays unless they are perfect trees
options.explanation: Any complete tree packs into an array with no gaps, including heaps whose last level is only partly filled. The problem is the index formulas, not the shape.

options.text: The parent formula should round up instead of down
options.explanation: Rounding up would still mismatch the child formulas. The real problem is that the 1-indexed formulas are being applied to a 0-indexed array.

options.text: Siblings must be kept in sorted order, and these formulas do not enforce that
options.explanation: A heap never orders siblings, under any index scheme. Only each parent and its children are compared.

questions.workedExample:
1. The common textbook layout puts the root at position 1. Then a node at position i has children at 2i and 2i + 1, and its parent at i halved and rounded down.
2. Python lists and most array code start at index 0. Using the same formulas there makes the root (index 0) its own left child, because 2 × 0 = 0, and the parent of index 1 comes out as 0 but so does the parent of index 0.
3. Shift everything by one to match a 0-based array: children at `2*i + 1` and `2*i + 2`, parent at `(i - 1) // 2`.
4. Quick check with index 10: parent `(10 - 1) // 2` is 4, children are 21 and 22, and both children's parent formula gives back 10.

options.text: `a[1]` is the second-smallest key
options.explanation: Not necessarily: the second smallest is a child of the root, so it is at index 1 **or** 2, depending on which side it ended up.

options.text: The second-smallest key is at index 1 or 2
options.explanation: Correct. The second smallest has only the minimum smaller than it, so its parent must be the root.

options.text: The leaves occupy the final half of the array, rounded up
options.explanation: Correct. A slot has a left child only when twice its index plus 1 is still inside the array, which is true exactly for the indices below n halved and rounded down.

options.explanation: The binary heap property only orders parents relative to children; the array as a whole is not sorted.

2. True: everything except the root has a parent smaller than itself; for the second smallest, the only smaller key is the root.
3. True. A slot is internal exactly when its left child's index, twice the slot index plus 1, is still inside the array. That holds only for the first half of the array (rounded down). With eight entries, index 3 has a child at 7, but index 4's would be at 9, past the end: indices 4 to 7 are leaves.
4. False: `[1, 3, 2]` again.
5. True: a key with a child cannot be the maximum, because the child is larger. So to find the max of a min-heap you check only the leaves, about half of the n items, which is still O(n).

lessons.title: Sift up, sift down and priority removal
lessons.summary: Push appends and moves the new key toward the root.
lessons.body:
Use the complete-tree array layout introduced earlier. The root is array slot zero; absent child positions lie beyond the occupied prefix. Here n counts binary heap entries and comparisons have constant cost. A valid min-heap makes each parent no greater than its children, without ordering siblings. Array allocation and returned output require their own cost accounting.

## Sift up: push

To push, append the new item at the end (the next free slot in the last level, which keeps the shape) and then **sift up**: while it is smaller than its parent, swap them.

```python
def sift_up(a, i):
    while i > 0:
        p = (i - 1) // 2
        # Stop once this parent-
        # child order holds.
        if a[p] <= a[i]:
            break
        a[p], a[i] = a[i], a[p]
        i = p

def push(a, x):
    a.append(x)
    sift_up(a, len(a) - 1)
```

Pushing 0 into the binary heap `[1, 3, 2, 4, 8, 7, 6, 9]` from the previous unit: it lands at index 8 (child of 4), swaps with 4, then 3, then 1, and becomes the new root. There is at most one swap per level, and because a heap is always a complete tree, it is short: a 9-item heap has height 3, so those 3 swaps are the most possible. A million-item binary heap has height 19, so push is **O(log n)**. Many pushes stop after one comparison, because a new item is often no smaller than its parent.

## Sift down: pop

To pop the minimum, you cannot just remove the root: that would leave a hole at the top. Instead, move the **last** item into the root (keeping the shape), shrink the array, and **sift down**: swap it with its **smaller** child until it is no larger than both children.

```python
def sift_down(a, i, n):
    while True:
        # Choose the smallest of
        # parent/children.
        best = i
        l, r = 2 * i + 1, 2 * i + 2
        if l < n and a[l] < a[best]:
            best = l
        if r < n and a[r] < a[best]:
            best = r
        if best == i:
            return
        a[i], a[best] = a[best], a[i]
        i = best

def pop(a):
    # Move the minimum to the
    # removable last slot.
    a[0], a[-1] = a[-1], a[0]
    top = a.pop()
    if a:
        sift_down(a, 0, len(a))
    return top
```

Swapping with the **smaller** child matters: that child becomes the parent of the other, so it must be the smaller of the two. Pop also makes at most one swap per level, the same height limit as push, so for n items it is also **O(log n)**.

> [!warning] Binary Heaps are not sorted
> Only `a[0]` is guaranteed to be the minimum. `a[1]` is not necessarily the second smallest (in the example it is 3, but 2 is smaller), and iterating over a binary heap list does not give sorted order. Popping repeatedly does.

## Key takeaways
- Push appends and moves the new key toward the root.
- Pop moves the final entry to the root and repairs downward.
- Choose the smaller child to preserve min-heap order.

## Further reading
- [Binary heap — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_heap)
- [Priority Queues — Algorithms, 4th ed. (Sedgewick & Wayne)](https://algs4.cs.princeton.edu/24pq/)

lessons.title: Bottom-up heapify and heapsort
lessons.summary: Build downward from the last internal node.
lessons.body:
Use the complete-tree array layout introduced earlier. The root is array slot zero; absent child positions lie beyond the occupied prefix. Here n counts binary heap entries and comparisons have constant cost. A valid min-heap makes each parent no greater than its children, without ordering siblings. Array allocation and returned output require their own cost accounting.

## Heapify in O(n)

Given n unsorted items, you could push them one at a time. Each push can climb the full height of the heap, so in the worst case (for example, pushing items in descending order into a min-heap) that is O(n log n): up to about 19 swaps for each of a million items. There is a faster way. Treat the array as a complete tree already, and sift down every **non-leaf** from the bottom up:

Use the sift_down helper from the preceding unit to execute heapify. Both operate in place on a list of comparable values; heapify does not return a new sorted list.

```python
def heapify(a):
    n = len(a)
    # Repair children before their parents.
    for i in range(n // 2 - 1, -1, -1):
        sift_down(a, i, n)
```

Trace on `[9, 4, 7, 1, 8, 2, 6, 3]` (8 items, so start at index 3):

```text-output
i=3 (1): children 3      no swap
i=2 (7): children 2, 6   swap with 2
i=1 (4): children 1, 8   swap with 1,
         then 4 vs 3     swap with 3
i=0 (9): children 1, 2   swap with 1,
         9 vs 3, 8       swap with 3,
         9 vs 4          swap with 4

result: [1, 3, 2, 4, 8, 7, 6, 9]
```

### Why is that O(n)?

The cost of sifting down a node is at most its **node height**, and most nodes have tiny heights. In a complete tree, half the nodes are leaves and never move. Of the rest, about a quarter of all nodes sit just above the leaves and can move down at most one level, an eighth at most two levels, and so on. Lots of short moves at the bottom and a few long ones at the top add up to fewer swaps than there are items:

```formula reference
S < n(1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + …) = n
where
S: the total number of swaps bottom-up heapify makes
n: the number of items
1/2, 1/4, 1/8: at most these fractions of the n nodes can move down at least one, two and three levels
…: "and so on": the fractions keep halving
In words: half the nodes can move down at least one level, a quarter at least two, an eighth at least three, and those halving counts add up to less than n swaps.
```

The trace above made 0 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 swaps for 8 items. For this sift-down, comparisons are bounded by about twice the item count (at most two child comparisons per level a node can move, including the final level where no swap is needed). Pushing one at a time is slower because new items arrive at the *bottom*, the level with the most nodes, and each may climb the full height.

The intuition: sift-down costs are cheap where nodes are plentiful (the bottom) and expensive only where they are rare (the top). Sift-up is the reverse.

### Heapsort

Heapify, then repeatedly swap the root with the last item and sift down over a shrinking prefix. That is **heapsort**: for n items, O(n log n) worst case (n pops, each sifting down at most the binary heap's height), O(1) extra memory, but not stable and with poor cache locality (child positions roughly double their parent position), which can affect practical performance. One use is the worst-case fallback inside **introsort** (the usual implementation of C++ `std::sort`), which switches to heapsort if quicksort recurses too deeply.

## Key takeaways
- Build downward from the last internal node.
- Most nodes can move only a few levels, making bottom-up heapify linear.
- Heapsort repeatedly repairs a shrinking binary heap and is not stable.

## Further reading
- [Priority Queues — Algorithms, 4th ed. (Sedgewick & Wayne)](https://algs4.cs.princeton.edu/24pq/)

lessons.summary: Use an insertion counter to break equal-priority payload ties.
lessons.body:
Use the complete-tree array layout introduced earlier. The root is array slot zero; absent child positions lie beyond the occupied prefix. Here n counts binary heap entries and comparisons have constant cost. A valid min-heap makes each parent no greater than its children, without ordering siblings. Array allocation and returned output require their own cost accounting.

## heapq in Python

Python's `heapq` module implements a **min-heap on a plain list**. There is no binary heap class.

Here n is the number of items in the binary heap (or in the input, for `heapify` and `nlargest`), and k is how many items you ask for.

| Function | Cost |
|---|---|
| `heappush(h, x)` | O(log n) |
| `heappop(h)` | O(log n) |
| `h[0]` (peek) | O(1) |
| `heapify(h)` | O(n), in place |
| `heapreplace(h, x)` | pop then push, O(log n) |
| `heappushpop(h, x)` | push then pop, O(log n) |
| `nlargest(k, it)` | O(n log(k + 1)) when k is between 1 and n; implementation may choose max or sorting |

Practical details:

- **Max-heaps**: before Python 3.14, negate the keys (`heappush(h, -x)`). Python 3.14 added `heapify_max`, `heappush_max`, `heappop_max` and friends.
- **Priorities with payloads**: push tuples `(priority, item)`. If two priorities tie, Python compares the items, which fails for objects that don't support `<`. Add a counter: `(priority, next(counter), item)`. This also makes ties first-in-first-out.
- **Changing a priority** ("decrease-key") is not supported. The usual trick is **lazy deletion**: push a new entry and mark the old one as removed, skipping stale entries when they are popped. Dijkstra's algorithm in Python is normally written this way.

## Pattern: top-k

"Find the k largest of n items" (top 10 search results, the 100 busiest IPs in a log). Sorting is O(n log n). Better: keep a **min-heap of size k** holding the best k seen so far. Its root is the *weakest* of the current top k, so each new item only needs comparing with the root.

```python
import heapq

def top_k(nums, k):
    if not isinstance(k, int) or k < 0:
        raise ValueError("k must be >= 0")
    if k == 0:
        return []
    h = []
    for x in nums:
        if len(h) < k:
            heapq.heappush(h, x)
        # Replace only the weakest
        # kept value.
        elif x > h[0]:
            heapq.heapreplace(h, x)
    return sorted(h, reverse=True)

top_k([5, 1, 9, 3, 7, 9, 2, 8], 3)
# [9, 9, 8]
```

Each item costs one comparison with the root, and at most one replace that sifts through a binary heap of only k items. Many items fail that first comparison and cost nothing more. So the worst case is O(n log(k + 1)) time, including the final sort of the k keepers, and O(k) memory (the + 1 just keeps the logarithm above zero when k is 1). Larger k returns all n items; zero keepers returns immediately.

With a billion log lines and 100 keepers, that is at most about 7 heap levels per item instead of the 30 a heap of all n items would need, and it works on a stream that never fits in memory. `heapq.nlargest` does this for you.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a door policy at a full venue
> A small venue holds exactly 100 people. Once it is full, the door staff let a newcomer in only if they beat the least impressive person currently inside, who is then asked to leave. The staff never need to compare a newcomer with anyone except that one weakest guest.
>
> **How it maps:** the venue is the min-heap of size k, the weakest guest is the root `h[0]`, the comparison at the door is `x > h[0]`, and the swap is `heapreplace`. Everyone turned away costs one comparison.
>
> **Where it stops:** door staff could simply know who is weakest. A heap must do a few swaps after each replacement, about log₂ k of them, to bring the next weakest keeper to the root.

> [!tip] Min-heap for the largest, max-heap for the smallest
> It feels backwards, but for the k **largest** you want quick access to the **smallest** of your keepers, because that is the one a newcomer must beat.

If all n items are in memory and you only need the k-th element, **quickselect** finds it in expected O(n), but it does not stream and reorders the array.

## Key takeaways
- Use an insertion counter to break equal-priority payload ties.
- A min-heap retains the largest stream items by exposing its weakest keeper.
- Changing priorities requires an extra policy such as lazy deletion.

## Further reading
- [heapq — Python docs](https://docs.python.org/3/library/heapq.html)

You must find the 50 largest response times in a stream of 100 million log lines, using little memory. Which approach fits best?

Here n is the number of input items, k counts kept items, and h names the binary min-heap list in the worked example.

options.text: Keep a max-heap of all items and pop 50 times
options.explanation: This stores all 10⁸ items in memory and costs O(n) to build; it ignores the 'little memory' requirement.

options.text: Sort all response times and take the last 50
options.explanation: O(n log n) time (n times its logarithm) and O(n) memory, and it cannot run on a stream without first storing everything.

options.text: Keep a max-heap of size 50 and push every item
options.explanation: A max-heap's root is the *largest* keeper, which tells you nothing about whether a new item should displace the *smallest* keeper.

options.text: Keep a min-heap of size 50; replace the root when a new item is larger
options.explanation: Correct. The root is the weakest of the current top 50, so each item needs one comparison and occasionally a replace that sifts through a binary heap only 6 levels deep. With k denoting the 50 kept items, that is O(n log k) time and O(k) memory.

questions.workedExample:
1. Maintain the best 50 seen so far.
2. The question for each new item is 'does it beat the worst of my 50?'. A **min-heap** answers that in O(1) at `h[0]`.
3. If it does, `heapreplace` swaps it in, sifting through a binary heap of 50 items, which has six node levels (at most five downward swaps).
4. Cost: after filling the min-heap, each later item makes one root comparison. A replacement in the simple downward-swap implementation traverses at most five edges; Python’s heapq may use a different repair procedure. The number of replacements depends on arrival order. Memory: 50 items.

`heapq.nlargest(50, stream)` implements exactly this.

questions.prompt:
This task queue crashes the first time two tasks share a priority. Why, and what is the standard fix?

```python
import heapq
q = []
heapq.heappush(q, (2, {"id": "a"}))
heapq.heappush(q, (2, {"id": "b"}))
```

options.text: heapq does not allow duplicate priorities; use a dict keyed by priority instead
options.explanation: heapq happily stores duplicates. The problem is what Python compares next when the first tuple elements tie.

options.text: The tuples tie on 2, so Python compares the dicts, which raises TypeError; insert a counter: `(2, next(counter), task)`
options.explanation: Correct. Tuples compare element by element. A unique, increasing counter in second place means the tasks themselves are never compared, and equal priorities come out first-in-first-out.

options.text: heapq requires a list of integers; store task IDs only
options.explanation: heapq works with any mutually comparable items, including tuples. Integers only is unnecessary.

options.text: The binary heap needs to be heapified after every push
options.explanation: heappush maintains the invariant itself; calling heapify afterwards wouldn't avoid the comparison that raises the error.

questions.workedExample:
1. Pushing the second tuple sifts it up, comparing `(2, {...b})` with `(2, {...a})`.
2. Tuple comparison: first elements equal (2 == 2), so compare second elements: two dicts.
3. `dict < dict` is not defined: `TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'dict' and 'dict'`.
4. Fix (as recommended in the heapq docs):

```python
import itertools
counter = itertools.count()
q = []  # rebuild after the failed push
for task in [{"id": "a"}, {"id": "b"}]:
    heapq.heappush(q,
        (2, next(counter), task))
```

The counter is unique, so comparison never reaches the task, and ties pop in insertion order.

options.text: On Python 3.14+, use `heapq.heapify_max`, `heappush_max` and `heappop_max`

options.text: Push `(-priority, counter, item)` tuples

options.explanation: The last element of a min-heap is just some leaf, not necessarily the maximum (the maximum is one of the leaves, roughly half of all the items).

lessons.title: Heap merging and alternative priority queues
lessons.summary: Keep only one current head from each sorted input.
lessons.body:
Use the complete-tree array layout introduced earlier. The root is array slot zero; absent child positions lie beyond the occupied prefix. Here n counts binary heap entries and comparisons have constant cost. A valid min-heap makes each parent no greater than its children, without ordering siblings. Array allocation and returned output require their own cost accounting.

## Pattern: k-way merge

Merge k sorted lists (sorted runs from an external sort, per-shard query results, SSTables in LSM-tree compaction). Put the head of each list in a min-heap; repeatedly pop the smallest and push the next item from the same list.

This function uses heapq; import it as in the previous unit before running the example. The sample call returns a list; the comment shows that returned list, rather than printed script output.

```python
def merge_k(lists):
    h = []
    for i, lst in enumerate(lists):
        if lst:
            h.append((lst[0], i, 0))
    heapq.heapify(h)
    out = []
    while h:
        val, i, j = heapq.heappop(h)
        out.append(val)
        # Advance only the list just popped.
        j += 1
        if j < len(lists[i]):
            nxt = (lists[i][j], i, j)
            heapq.heappush(h, nxt)
    return out

merge_k([[1, 4, 9], [2, 3, 10], [5]])
# [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 9, 10]
```

The binary heap never holds more than k items, one current head per list, so each of the N output items costs one pop and at most one push through a small heap of about log₂ k levels. That is O(k + N log(k + 1)) time, including scanning empty input lists, with O(k) heap space plus O(N) returned output. Two simpler alternatives are much worse when k is large: scanning all k heads to find each next item costs about k comparisons per item, and merging the lists pairwise one after another can re-copy early items about k times, up to O(N·k), N times k. `heapq.merge` is a lazy version of the heap merge.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: merging sorted piles of post
> Several sorters each hand you a pile of letters already in postcode order. To make one sorted stack you only ever look at the top letter of each pile: take the smallest, then reveal the next letter from that same pile.
>
> **How it maps:** each pile is a sorted input list, the visible top letters are the heap's contents (one head per list), taking the smallest is `heappop`, and revealing the next letter from that pile is the push from the same list.
>
> **Where it stops:** with three piles you can spot the smallest top letter at a glance. With a thousand piles, scanning every top would take a thousand looks per letter; the heap keeps the tops arranged so each step walks only about ten levels of the heap.

## Beyond binary heaps

- **d-ary heaps** (4-ary is common) are shallower, reducing possible upward levels but requiring more child comparisons per downward level. Cache and runtime effects depend on the implementation and workload.
- Fibonacci heaps support amortised O(1) decrease-key and O(log n) delete-min (for n queued items), giving O(E + V log V) for Dijkstra on a graph with V vertices and E edges, with suitable handles and nonnegative edge weights. Ordinary pairing heaps do not share this combined constant-amortized decrease-key guarantee; their analysis is different. Benchmark concrete implementations before choosing.
- Real uses: OS timer queues, Go's `container/heap`, Java's `PriorityQueue` (a binary heap), job schedulers, and the event queue in network simulators.

## Key takeaways
- Keep only one current head from each sorted input.
- After popping a head, advance only its input.
- Different priority queue structures trade off child comparisons and update costs.

## Further reading
- [heapq — Python docs](https://docs.python.org/3/library/heapq.html)
- [K-way merge algorithm — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K-way_merge_algorithm)

lessons.title: Trie paths, exact lookup and prefixes
lessons.summary: Shared prefixes share a root-to-node path.
lessons.body:
In this lesson L is the length of a key in characters and n is the number of keys stored. Hash-table lookup uses expected O(1) probes (a fixed number on average) under suitable hashing assumptions; hashing and equality on uncached strings can cost O(L), in proportion to the key's length. They cannot answer "which words **start with** `inte`?" without scanning every key. Balanced BSTs can, but each step of the search is a whole string comparison: about 20 comparisons for a million keys, each of which may read the full key. So a BST lookup costs O(L log n) in the worst case, and the trie below brings that down to O(L): it reads each character of the key once. Real string comparisons often stop at the first differing character, so the BST figure is a worst case.

A **trie** (from re*trie*val, usually pronounced "try") is built for prefix questions. Instead of storing whole keys in nodes, it stores **one character per edge**. A key is a path from the root, and every key that shares a prefix shares the path for that prefix.

## The structure

Here is a trie holding `car`, `card`, `care`, `cat`, `do` and `dog`. A `*` marks a node where a word ends.

```
          (root)
          /    \
         c      d
         |      |
         a      o*
        / \     |
       r*  t*   g*
      / \
     d*  e*
```

Things to notice:

- The root represents the empty string. Each node represents the prefix spelled by the path to it.
- `car` and `card` share three nodes. Shared prefixes are stored once.
- `do` is a word *and* a prefix of `dog`, so an end-of-word **flag** is needed; you cannot rely on "is it a leaf?".
- Keys are never compared with each other. Lookup cost depends on the **length of the key**, not on how many keys are stored.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: signposts that spell a word
> Imagine a town where every road junction has signposts labelled with single letters. To reach "card" you take the C turning, then A, then R, then D. Some junctions also carry a plaque saying "a destination ends here".
>
> **How it maps:** junctions are trie nodes, each lettered turning is an edge, the route you drive is the key, and the plaque is the end-of-word flag. Everyone heading to a word starting "car" shares the same first three roads, which is how a trie stores shared prefixes once.
>
> **Where it stops:** a real junction has only a few turnings. A trie node may need room for every possible next character, which is why tries can use a lot of memory (the trie-memory unit).

## Insert, search and prefix queries

```python
class Node:
    def __init__(self):
        self.kids = {}    # char -> Node
        self.end = False  # word ends here

def insert(root, word):
    node = root
    for ch in word:
        if ch not in node.kids:
            node.kids[ch] = Node()
        # Shared prefixes reuse
        # existing nodes.
        node = node.kids[ch]
    # The path may also prefix longer words.
    node.end = True

def walk(root, s):
    node = root
    for ch in s:
        node = node.kids.get(ch)
        if node is None:
            return None
    return node

def search(root, word):
    node = walk(root, word)
    return bool(node and node.end)

def starts_with(root, prefix):
    return walk(root, prefix) is not None
```

With the trie above:

| Call | Result | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `search(root, "car")` | True | path exists, flag set |
| `search(root, "ca")` | False | path exists, no flag |
| `starts_with(root, "ca")` | True | path exists |
| `search(root, "dot")` | False | no `t` under `do` |

With constant-time child access, insertion, exact lookup and prefix-path lookup take O(L + 1) for a key or prefix of L characters: one step per character, plus the root (the + 1 covers the empty string, for zero characters). The dict-backed example uses expected constant-time child lookups. For an empty prefix, `starts_with` returns True even on an empty trie because the root exists; this tests path existence, not whether any word is stored.

> [!note] O(L) is not automatically faster than hashing
> Hashing a previously unhashed string inspects its characters; some runtimes cache string hashes, and equality costs also matter. Tries directly support prefix navigation and can stop early on a miss. Practical exact-match performance depends on representation and workload.

## Key takeaways
- Shared prefixes share a root-to-node path.
- An end flag distinguishes complete words from their prefixes.
- Lookup follows key characters with expected constant-cost dictionary access.

## Further reading
- [Trie — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trie)
- [Tries — Algorithms, 4th ed. (Sedgewick & Wayne)](https://algs4.cs.princeton.edu/52trie/)

lessons.title: Enumerating and ranking completions
lessons.summary: Walk to the prefix node before enumerating descendants.
lessons.body:
A character trie starts at an always-present root representing the empty prefix. Earlier units used Node.kids as a dictionary of character-to-child links and Node.end as the complete-word flag. Here L counts characters in the searched string or prefix and n counts stored keys. Dictionary child access is expected constant time, rather than a worst-case guarantee.

## Autocomplete

Autocomplete is "walk to the prefix node, then enumerate words below it".

Run this function with the Node, insert and walk definitions from the lookup unit. Populate the trie with car, card, care, cat, do and dog to obtain the illustrative completion list below.

```python
def complete(root, prefix, limit=10):
    if not isinstance(limit, int):
        raise TypeError("integer limit")
    if limit < 0:
        raise ValueError("limit >= 0")
    out = []
    def dfs(node, path):
        if len(out) == limit:
            return
        if node.end:
            out.append(path)
        # Sorting gives code-point
        # word order.
        for ch in sorted(node.kids):
            if len(out) >= limit:
                break
            dfs(node.kids[ch], path + ch)
    start = walk(root, prefix)
    if start:
        dfs(start, prefix)
    return out

# complete(root, "ca")
# ['car', 'card', 'care', 'cat']
```

Sorted child traversal produces Python string lexicographic order (code-point order, not locale-aware alphabetical collation). This simple implementation copies path strings and sorts child keys during recursion; enumeration costs include visited nodes, copied characters and output, and deep words can hit Python's recursion limit.

An autocomplete design may rank by popularity. Enumerating and sorting every match can be expensive, so one option is to cache top-k word IDs at selected prefix nodes. Looking up such a cached list of k IDs for a prefix of L characters costs expected O(L + k) in this representation, excluding retrieval and transmission of the completion text. The trade-off is memory, and slower updates when popularity changes.

> [!example] Sizing an autocomplete trie
> In a hypothetical dataset, 10 million queries with mean length exactly 20 have 200 million characters in total, but shared prefixes typically cut the node count substantially. Storing the top 10 completions at every node as 4-byte IDs adds 40 bytes per node, before container overhead. A design can store these lists only at selected shallow nodes and compute other results on demand; the best policy depends on query traffic.

## Key takeaways
- Walk to the prefix node before enumerating descendants.
- Sorted child traversal gives code-point order, not locale-aware collation.
- Cached top completions exchange update and memory costs for query speed.

## Further reading
