options.explanation: Tries aren't balanced trees and aren't searched by comparison; the walk length is the prefix length.

options.text: O(50,000,000 log 10), a top-k binary heap over every query
options.explanation: That re-scans the whole log per keystroke. The point of storing top-k at each node is to do this work offline.

questions.workedExample:
1. Walk L characters to the prefix node: O(L).
2. Read the node's stored top-10 list: O(10).
3. Total O(L + k), where L counts prefix characters and k counts the ten stored IDs; this does not imply any fixed microsecond latency.

The cost moves elsewhere:
- **Memory**: k entries at every node. Systems often store lists only for short prefixes (which most keystrokes hit) and compute rare deep ones on demand.
- **Updates**: when popularity changes, the lists on the path from the query's node up to the root may need recomputing, so it is usually rebuilt offline in batches.

lessons.title: Child representations and trie memory
lessons.summary: Child arrays reserve every alphabet position even when unused.
lessons.body:
A character trie starts at an always-present root representing the empty prefix. Earlier units used Node.kids as a dictionary of character-to-child links and Node.end as the complete-word flag. Here L counts characters in the searched string or prefix and n counts stored keys. Dictionary child access is expected constant time, rather than a worst-case guarantee.

## The memory problem

Tries are fast but notoriously **memory-hungry**, because every character of every unshared suffix gets its own node, and each node carries overhead.

Common child representations differ in how much they reserve per node. An array of child pointers reserves one slot for every possible character, used or not: with 8-byte pointers, a node for lowercase English reserves 26 slots, 208 bytes, and a node for arbitrary bytes reserves 256 slots, 2 KiB (2,048 bytes), before any object header.

| Children as | Lookup | Memory per node |
|---|---|---|
| Array of 26 (or 256) pointers | O(1) index | 208 B (or 2 KiB) with 8-byte pointers, mostly empty |
| Hash map / dict | O(1) expected | Small, but high constant overhead |
| Sorted list | O(log σ) | Compact |

Here σ (sigma) is the alphabet size, and O(log σ) is the cost of a binary search among at most σ sorted children. A tree of N nodes has only N − 1 child links in total, so in a 26-slot array trie only about one slot in 26 ever holds a child, whatever the words are. Dictionary and node object sizes vary by language and interpreter build, so measure before choosing between the compact options.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a rack of letter trays at every desk
> An office gives every desk a rack of 26 letter trays, one per letter of the alphabet, so post can be filed instantly. But most desks only ever receive post in one or two trays, and the racks take up more room than the post.
>
> **How it maps:** each desk is a trie node, each tray is a child-pointer slot, and post arriving is a child that actually exists. Instant filing is the O(1) array lookup; the empty trays are the wasted slots.
>
> **Where it stops:** an office could share racks between desks. A trie node's slots belong to that node alone, so the only cures are to store just the children that exist or to merge chains of single-child nodes.

With long mostly unshared suffixes, many nonterminal trie nodes have exactly one child: the unshared tail of a single word like `...ication`. That observation drives the fix.

## Why uniform hashes share little structure

SHA-256 values use 64 hexadecimal characters when encoded as hex. Imagine storing one million independent, approximately uniform hashes in a character trie. Each additional character multiplies the possible prefixes by sixteen, so the keys run out of company quickly:

- At depth 5 there are just over a million possible prefixes, about one per key, so many keys still share: only about 39 % have a 5-character prefix to themselves.
- By depth 7 there are 268 million possible prefixes, and about 99.6 % of keys are alone.
- From there to character 64, almost every key owns a private chain of single-child nodes.

Adding up the expected number of distinct prefixes at every depth gives about 60 million nodes for a million keys: roughly 60 nodes per key, each carrying its own child structure. A radix tree compresses those long private suffixes, but a hash set is usually the first structure to consider when the task needs only exact membership and no prefix queries.

## Key takeaways
- Child arrays reserve every alphabet position even when unused.
- Dictionary and object overhead depends on the implementation.
- Mostly unshared suffixes make character tries poor exact-match indexes.

## Further reading
- [Trie — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trie)
- [Tries — Algorithms, 4th ed. (Sedgewick & Wayne)](https://algs4.cs.princeton.edu/52trie/)

questions.prompt: A word-lookup service stores lowercase English words in a trie whose nodes each hold an **array of 26 child pointers**. It has about a million nodes, and memory profiling shows about 200 MB in the child arrays alone, almost all of it null pointers. Which change attacks the cause most directly?

options.text: Store only the children that exist, in a small map or sorted list, and compress single-child chains
options.explanation: Correct. A tree of N nodes has only N − 1 child links, so about 25 of every 26 array slots are empty. Storing only real children removes that waste, and compressing chains (a radix tree) also removes most of the nodes.

options.text: Widen each node to 256 slots so that any byte can be stored
options.explanation: That makes each node about ten times bigger, and nearly all the new slots would also be empty.

options.text: Switch to 4-byte pointers or indices
options.explanation: Halving each slot halves the waste but leaves the cause: each node still reserves 26 slots when it typically uses one.

options.text: Add an end-of-word flag to each node
options.explanation: Tries already need that flag to tell words from prefixes. It adds a little memory and does nothing about empty child slots.

questions.workedExample:
1. Each node reserves 26 pointer slots, 208 bytes with 8-byte pointers, so a million nodes need about 208 MB for the arrays, whatever words are stored.
2. A tree of N nodes has exactly N − 1 parent-child links. Spread over 26 slots per node, only about one slot in 26 can ever be used.
3. So the cost comes from reserving slots for children that do not exist. The direct fix is to store only real children: a small hash map or a sorted list of (character, child) pairs.
4. Many trie nodes also sit on single-child chains (unshared word endings). A radix tree merges those chains into labelled edges, cutting the node count as well.

Smaller pointers or adding flags only change constants; they keep reserving space for the 25 missing children.

questions.prompt: You need to store one million independent, approximately uniform SHA-256 values (64 hex characters each) and test membership. A colleague suggests a character trie "because tries are fast for strings". What is the main problem with that plan, and what should you use instead?

options.text: None: the trie stores one node per key, so it is as compact as a hash set
options.explanation: A trie stores one node per distinct prefix, not per key. Random hashes share almost nothing beyond the first few characters, so each key needs its own long chain.

options.text: The trie can hold only 64 nodes, one per character position, so most keys will not fit
options.explanation: Nodes are per distinct *prefix*, not per position. There are millions of different prefixes after just a few characters.

options.text: Random hashes stop sharing prefixes after about 5 to 7 characters, so each key needs a private chain of nearly 60 nodes, about 60 million in total; use a hash set
options.explanation: Correct. With 16 choices per character, the number of possible prefixes passes a million at depth 5, and by depth 7 almost every key is alone. The rest of each hash becomes a single-child chain. A hash set stores each key once and answers exact membership directly.

options.text: Tries cannot store hexadecimal digits, only letters
options.explanation: A trie can use any alphabet; a hex trie simply has up to 16 children per node.

questions.workedExample:
1. Each extra hex character multiplies the possible prefixes by 16. At depth 5 there are just over a million possible prefixes, about one per key, so many keys still share a path: only about 39 % are alone there.
2. By depth 7 there are about 268 million possible prefixes and about 99.6 % of keys have a path to themselves.
3. From there to character 64, each key's remaining characters form a private chain of single-child nodes. Adding up the expected distinct prefixes at every depth gives about 60 million nodes, roughly 60 per key.
4. Exact membership with no prefix queries does not need a trie at all: a hash set stores each key once (or a Bloom filter, if false positives are acceptable). A radix tree would also collapse the chains, with different memory and update trade-offs that would need measuring.

lessons.title: Compressed paths, routing and trie variants
lessons.summary: Compress single-child chains only when no intermediate key ends there.
lessons.body:
A character trie starts at an always-present root representing the empty prefix. Earlier units used Node.kids as a dictionary of character-to-child links and Node.end as the complete-word flag. Here L counts characters in the searched string or prefix and n counts stored keys. Dictionary child access is expected constant time, rather than a worst-case guarantee.

## Compressed tries and radix trees

A **radix tree** (also called a compressed trie, or a **Patricia** trie in its binary form) merges chains of single-child nodes that do not mark a key end into one edge labelled with a **string** rather than a character.

```
 trie              radix tree
  c                 "ca"
  |                 /   \
  a              "r"*   "t"*
 / \             /  \
r*  t*         "d"*  "e"*
/ \
d* e*
```

- Except possibly the root, every internal node now has at least two children (or marks a word end), so the node count is at most twice the number of stored keys, independent of key length (see below).
- Lookups compare chunks of characters along each edge, with the same O(L) total for a key of L characters.
- Inserting can **split** an edge: adding `cab` to the tree above splits nothing because `ca` already exists, but adding `co` would split `ca` into `c` with children `a` and `o`.

The node bound comes from counting the only kinds of node compression leaves behind: nodes that mark a key end (at most one per key), branching nodes (always fewer than the number of keys, as in any tree whose branch points have at least two children), and the root. So a radix tree holding at least one key has at most about twice as many nodes as keys, however long the keys are. The radix tree drawn above holds 4 keys (car, card, care, cat) in 5 labelled nodes plus the root. A plain trie, by contrast, can need one node per character of every key.

Radix trees are where tries meet production. Many of these uses rely on **longest prefix match**: among all stored prefixes of a lookup key, pick the longest.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: the most specific delivery rule wins
> A parcel depot has rules such as "anything for Leeds goes to van 1" and "anything for Park Lane, Leeds goes to van 4". A letter for 10 Park Lane, Leeds matches both, and the more specific rule wins. A letter for another Leeds street matches only the first.
>
> **How it maps:** each rule is a stored prefix with a route attached, the address is the lookup key read from the general part to the specific, and choosing the most specific matching rule is longest prefix match. Walking a trie and remembering the last rule passed finds it in one pass.
>
> **Where it stops:** delivery rules match names, and a person can read the whole address at once. A router matches a fixed number of address bits, from the most significant bit down, and has to make the decision for millions of packets a second.

- **IP routing**: a router finds the **longest prefix match** of a destination address against a table of CIDR prefixes. Binary tries over address bits, compressed (Patricia, LC-tries), are a classic implementation; Linux's IPv4 routing table uses an LC-trie (`fib_trie`).
- **HTTP routers**: Go's `httprouter` and many others match URL paths with a radix tree.
- Redis Streams use a radix tree of listpacks; a radix-tree entry represents a packed group of stream entries rather than necessarily one node per message.
- **Ethereum** stores its world state in a Merkle Patricia trie.
- The Linux page cache historically used a "radix tree", now the **XArray**, to map file offsets to pages.

## Other variants, briefly

- **Ternary search trees** store one character per node with less/equal/greater children, like a BST over characters. They use far less memory than array tries and still support prefix search.
- **Suffix tries and suffix trees** hold every suffix of a text, answering "does pattern P occur anywhere?" in time proportional to the length of P, written O(|P|), where |P| is the number of characters in the pattern. Suffix arrays are the space-efficient alternative.
- **Aho–Corasick** adds failure links to a trie of patterns, finding all occurrences of many patterns in one pass over a text (GNU grep uses it for multiple fixed patterns, and intrusion-detection systems can use it to match many signatures).
- Finite-state transducers can merge equivalent states and share suitable suffix structure as well as prefixes. Compression depends on the vocabulary and outputs.

## When to reach for a trie

Use one when you need:

- prefix queries: autocomplete, "all keys under `/api/v1/`", routing;
- longest-prefix matching;
- many patterns matched at once (Aho–Corasick);
- sorted iteration over strings with shared prefixes.

Avoid one when you only do exact-match lookups (use a hash set), when keys share few prefixes (random IDs, hashes: the trie degenerates into one long chain per key), or when memory is tight and a sorted array with binary search on prefixes will do.

## Key takeaways
- Compress single-child chains only when no intermediate key ends there.
- Insertion may split an edge at the first different character.
- Routing uses the longest matching prefix, while exact membership often suits hashing.

## Further reading
- [Radix tree — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radix_tree)
- [Longest prefix match — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Longest_prefix_match)
- [Ternary search tree — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ternary_search_tree)
- [Aho–Corasick algorithm — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aho%E2%80%93Corasick_algorithm)
- [Fixed-pattern search performance — GNU grep manual](https://www.gnu.org/software/grep/manual/html_node/Performance.html)

options.text: Listing every stored key that begins with `/api/v2/`
options.explanation: Correct. A trie walks to the prefix node in O(L + 1), where L counts prefix characters, then enumerates only the matching keys; a hash set must scan every key.

options.text: Checking whether an exact key is present, as fast as possible
options.explanation: Exact membership does not require prefix structure. Performance depends on cached hashes, collisions, allocation and representation; no universal speed winner follows.

options.text: Finding the longest stored prefix of a given string, as in IP routing
options.explanation: Correct. Walk down the trie, remembering the last flagged node. A hash set would need one lookup per possible prefix length.

options.text: Iterating over keys in lexicographic order
options.explanation: Correct. A pre-order walk visiting children in order yields sorted keys; a hash set has no order.

options.text: Storing a million random 64-character hashes compactly
options.explanation: Random keys share almost no prefixes, so a trie spends a node per character per key. A plain character trie has a much larger node count; actual byte use depends on the representations.

1. Prefix enumeration: the trie's reason for existing. Trie.
2. Exact match: no intrinsic prefix-navigation benefit; benchmark the representations.
3. Longest prefix: walk once, remember the deepest word-end seen. Trie (this is how routing tables use them).
4. Sorted iteration: trie (or a balanced BST). Hash sets are unordered.
5. Random keys: the trie becomes a forest of long single-child chains, costing tens of millions of nodes. Hash set.

options.explanation: Correct. The insert finds the common prefix `te`, splits the existing edge there, and adds the remainders as two child edges.

options.text: Root → `"t"` → `"e"`, then `"st"` and `"am"`

2. **Split** the edge: root → `te` → (remainder `st`, flagged as a word end).

questions.prompt: A router's table has three routes: `10.0.0.0/8 → A`, `10.1.0.0/16 → B` and `10.1.2.0/24 → C`. A packet arrives for `10.1.3.7`. Using longest-prefix match (as a binary trie over address bits does), which route is chosen?

options.explanation: Routing uses the *most specific* matching prefix, not the first. /8 matches, but so does /16.

options.text: C, because /24 is the most specific route
options.explanation: The /24 covers only 10.1.2.0–10.1.2.255. 10.1.3.7 is outside it, so it isn't a match at all.

options.text: None; the packet is dropped
options.explanation: At least the /8 matches, and /16 does too. A miss only happens if no prefix (and no default route) matches.

options.text: B, the longest prefix that actually matches
options.explanation: Correct. 10.1.3.7 starts with 10 (/8) and 10.1 (/16), but not 10.1.2 (/24). The longest match is /16.

1. Check each route:

| Route | Covers | Match? |
|---|---|---|
| /8 → A | 10.*.*.* | yes |
| /16 → B | 10.1.*.* | yes |
| /24 → C | 10.1.2.* | no |

2. Longest matching prefix: /16, so **B**.

questions.prompt: For at least one stored key and a nonempty lookup key, with constant-cost child access, which statements about radix trees (compressed tries) are true? Here n counts stored keys and L counts lookup characters. Select all that apply.

options.text: Every node either marks the end of a key or has at least two children (apart from possibly the root)
options.explanation: Correct. Any node with one child and no word ending would be merged with its child, by definition of the compression.

options.explanation: Correct. There are at most one word-end node per stored key, fewer branching nodes than keys, and a possibly separate root, for at most twice the key count in total, whereas a plain trie can need a node per character.

options.text: Lookups are O(L), the same order as a plain trie
options.explanation: Correct. You still compare every character of the key, just in chunks along edge labels.

options.text: They answer prefix queries more slowly than a hash set
options.explanation: Prefix queries are what tries are for. A hash set has to scan every key to answer one.

lessons.title: Lowest common ancestors in ordered and general trees
lessons.summary: A BST query follows the side containing both keys until they split.
lessons.body:
Tree problems look endlessly varied, but nearly all of them use one of a few patterns. Learn the patterns and most "new" problems become variations.

1. **Post-order combine.** Each call returns a summary of its subtree (height, sum, "found it?"), and the parent combines its children's summaries. Often a second value, the global best, is tracked on the side.
2. **Pre-order with state passed down.** Each call receives information from above (a running sum, a valid range, a depth) and passes an updated version to its children.
3. **Level-order** when the question mentions levels, widths or nearest anything.

This lesson works through the classics. Assume finite acyclic binary trees without shared nodes or concurrent mutation. These recursive examples are limited by Python call depth. Time bounds use unit-cost arithmetic; hashing-based bounds are expected. Throughout, n is the number of nodes and h is the tree's height in edges. Working recursion depth is O(h + 1), but dictionaries, serialized text and returned trees can require additional storage.

## Lowest common ancestor

The **lowest common ancestor** (LCA) of nodes p and q is the deepest node that has both as descendants (a node counts as its own descendant). It underlies "how are these two related?" questions: the nearest shared directory of two files, merge bases of Git commits (a DAG can have several incomparable best common ancestors, unlike a rooted tree), or the distance between two nodes. The path from p to q climbs from p up to their LCA, then goes down to q, so the distance between two nodes follows directly from their depths once you know the LCA:

```formula reference
d(p, q) = D(p) + D(q) − 2D(a)
where
p, q: the two nodes being compared
a: their lowest common ancestor
D(x): the depth of node x: its number of edges below the root
d(p, q): the distance between p and q: the number of edges on the path joining them
In words: climb from p up to the common ancestor, then down to q; each leg is a difference in depths, and together they give depth(p) + depth(q) minus twice the ancestor's depth.
```

For example, nodes 3 and 5 in the BST drawn below both have depth 3, and their LCA, 4, has depth 2: one edge up from 3 to 4 and one edge down to 5, so they are 2 edges apart. Get the LCA wrong and the distance comes out wrong too.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: the smallest area containing two addresses
> Two houses on the same street share that street; two on different streets in the same town share only the town; two in different towns may share only the county. The smallest area containing both tells you how they are related, and how far up you must go before coming back down.
>
> **How it maps:** areas nested inside areas form a tree, each house is a node, and the smallest area containing both houses is their lowest common ancestor. Going up from one house to that area and down to the other is the path between the two nodes.
>
> **Where it stops:** real boundaries overlap and change, while a tree gives every node exactly one parent. And areas have no ordering, so finding the shared area needs a search like the general-tree algorithm below, not the BST shortcut.

### In a BST: follow the split

```
          6
        /   \
       2     8
      / \   / \
     0   4 7   9
        / \
       3   5
```

If p and q are both smaller than the current node, the LCA is on the left; both larger, on the right. Otherwise they **split** here (or one of them *is* this node), so this node is the LCA.

```python
def lca_bst(root, p, q):
    node = root
    while node:
        if p < node.val and q < node.val:
            node = node.left
        elif p > node.val and q > node.val:
            node = node.right
        else:
            return node    # split point
```

Assume unique ordered keys and that both queried keys exist in this tree. The function does not verify membership.

`lca_bst(root, 3, 5)` is 4, `lca_bst(root, 2, 8)` is 6 and `lca_bst(root, 0, 5)` is 2. This is O(h) time for a tree of height h, with O(1) space (a fixed amount, just the current node).

### In any binary tree: post-order

Without ordering, ask each subtree "did you find p or q?":

```python
def lca(node, p, q):
    # p and q are node objects
    if (node is None or node is p or
            node is q):
        return node
    left = lca(node.left, p, q)
    right = lca(node.right, p, q)
    if left and right:
        return node        # p, q split
    # Carry a find upward if only one
    # side found.
    return left or right
```

If both sides report a find, this node is where the paths diverge. If only one does, pass its result up. When p is an ancestor of q, the search returns p as soon as it reaches it without looking below, which is correct because p is then the LCA. (This version assumes both nodes are in the tree; if either might be missing, count the finds explicitly.)

## Key takeaways
- A BST query follows the side containing both keys until they split.
- A general tree combines findings from its two children.
- The simple algorithms assume both requested nodes belong to the tree.

## Further reading
- [Lowest common ancestor — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lowest_common_ancestor)

lessons.title: Many ancestor queries with preprocessing
lessons.summary: Binary lifting stores power-of-two ancestor jumps.
lessons.body:
Use the binary Node with val, left and right fields introduced earlier. Assume a finite acyclic tree with no shared nodes or concurrent mutation. Throughout this unit n counts nodes and h is the tree height in edges. Recursive examples are limited by Python call depth; arithmetic has unit cost and hash-table operations have expected constant cost. Each example distinguishes working storage from returned output.

## Many queries

For millions of LCA queries on a fixed tree of n nodes, each O(n) walk is too slow. Two standard upgrades:

- **Binary lifting**: precompute, for every node, its ancestors 1, 2, 4, 8, … levels up, in O(n log n) time. Then lift the deeper node to the same depth and jump both up together in powers of two: O(log n) per query.
- **Euler tour + range minimum**: record a node and its depth on entry and again after returning from each child (not just DFS preorder); the LCA is the shallowest node between the first visits of p and q. With a sparse table, queries become O(1) after O(n log n) preprocessing. (Range-query structures such as segment and Fenwick trees are covered in the advanced module.)

The binary-lifting table is built from itself: two half-size jumps make one full-size jump. The ancestor 8 levels up is the ancestor 4 levels above the ancestor 4 levels up, so each level of the table comes from the one before. Give the root itself as its parent, or handle a missing-ancestor sentinel consistently, so upward jumps remain defined.

```formula reference
A_k(v) = A_{k−1}(A_{k−1}(v))
where
v: any node
k: the table level, from 1 upwards; level 0 holds each node's parent
A_k(v): the ancestor of v that is 2^k levels above it (k copies of 2 multiplied together: 2, 4, 8, …)
A_{k−1}(v): the ancestor 2^(k−1) levels above v, from the previous level of the table
In words: each jump stored in the table is two jumps of half that size from the level before, so the whole table is built level by level from the parents.
```

For 100,000 nodes that is 17 levels and 1.7 million table entries. Any climb of up to 99,999 levels is split into powers of two, like writing the number in binary: a climb of 13 is 8 + 4 + 1, three jumps. So no climb needs more than 17 jumps.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: express lifts in a tall building
> A tower has lifts that go up 1, 2, 4, 8 or 16 floors at a time. To go up 13 floors you take the 8, then the 4, then the 1: three rides instead of thirteen stops.
>
> **How it maps:** floors are levels in the tree, each express lift is one level of the binary-lifting table, and choosing lifts by the binary digits of the distance is how a query climbs. The LCA query lifts the deeper node to the other's level, then takes the biggest jumps that keep both nodes below their common ancestor.
>
> **Where it stops:** a building shares one set of lifts. The table stores a separate set of jumps for every node, which is why it costs memory in proportion to the number of nodes times the number of levels, and it must be rebuilt if the tree changes.

## Key takeaways
- Binary lifting stores power-of-two ancestor jumps.
- An Euler depth tour converts ancestor queries to range minima.
- Preprocessing pays off when a fixed tree serves many queries.

## Further reading
- [Lowest Common Ancestor (Euler tour) — cp-algorithms](https://cp-algorithms.com/graph/lca.html)
- [LCA with binary lifting — cp-algorithms](https://cp-algorithms.com/graph/lca_binary_lifting.html)
- [Euler tour technique — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euler_tour_technique)

questions.prompt: A service stores a fixed rooted hierarchy of 100,000 entries (some lineages are thousands of generations deep in its synthetic test data) and must answer 1,000,000 "closest common ancestor" queries a day. Which approaches give O(log n) or faster per query, with at most O(n log n) preprocessing? Select all that apply. Here n is the number of hierarchy entries.

options.text: Run the recursive `lca` from the root for each query
options.explanation: Each query may walk the whole tree: O(n) per query, about 10¹¹ steps per day.

options.text: Binary lifting: precompute power-of-two ancestor jumps, then climb using those jumps
options.explanation: Correct. Each successive table level doubles the jump distance, so the table holds each node's ancestors 1, 2, 4, 8, … levels up. O(n log n) preprocessing (about 1.7 million entries) and O(log n) query time: about 34 table levels to inspect across alignment and paired climbing.

options.text: Precompute a table of the LCA for every pair of people
options.explanation: Queries would be O(1), but 10⁵ × 10⁵ = 10¹⁰ pairs is O(n²) preprocessing and far too much memory.

options.text: Euler tour plus a sparse table for range-minimum queries on depth
options.explanation: Correct. O(n log n) to build the sparse table, then O(1) per query: the LCA is the shallowest node between the first visits of p and q.

options.text: Give every node a parent pointer and walk both nodes up to equal depth, then up together
options.explanation: This is O(depth) per query. With lineages thousands of generations deep, depth is not O(log n).

questions.workedExample:
1. Naive DFS can inspect all 100,000 nodes per query, for a scale of 100 billion node visits across one million queries.
2. Binary lifting:
   - Build the table level by level (in code, `up[k][v] = up[k-1][up[k-1][v]]`): two jumps of half the size make each jump. 17 levels cover any depth in a 100,000-node tree, so the table has about 1.7 million entries, built in O(n log n).
   - Query: lift the deeper node to equal depth, then jump both while their ancestors differ: about 34 steps.
3. All-pairs table: 10¹⁰ entries. Out.
4. Euler tour + sparse table: O(n log n) build, O(1) query. In.
5. Parent-pointer walk: O(depth), which here can be thousands of steps. That's the step binary lifting accelerates.

lessons.title: Diameter from one post-order pass
lessons.summary: A longest path can bend below the root.
lessons.body:
Use the binary Node with val, left and right fields introduced earlier. Assume a finite acyclic tree with no shared nodes or concurrent mutation. Throughout this unit n counts nodes and h is the tree height in edges. Recursive examples are limited by Python call depth; arithmetic has unit cost and hash-table operations have expected constant cost. Each example distinguishes working storage from returned output.

## Diameter

The **diameter** is the number of edges on the longest path between any two nodes. The trap: that path need **not** pass through the root.

```
          1
         /
        2
       / \
      3   6
     /     \
    4       7
   /         \
  5           8
```

The longest path here is 5–4–3–2–6–7–8: 6 edges, bending at node 2. The root is not on it.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: the longest walk on a branching trail
> A park's trails branch out from a car park and never loop. The longest walk between any two trail ends usually bends at some junction deep in the park, running out to the far end of one branch and the far end of another. It need not pass the car park at all.
>
> **How it maps:** junctions and trail ends are nodes, trail sections are edges and the car park is the root. The longest walk is the diameter, and the junction where it turns is the path's highest node.
>
> **Where it stops:** real trails can join up into loops, giving several routes between two points. In a tree there is exactly one path between any two nodes, which is why measuring one bend per node is enough.

Every path has a single highest node where it bends. At that node it goes down one edge into each subtree and then as deep as that subtree allows. So the best path bending at a node is the two subtree heights added together, plus the two edges into them. At node 2 above, both subtrees have height 2, giving the 6-edge path; at a leaf such as 5, both sides are empty (height −1), giving 0. The diameter is the largest of these values over all nodes, so compute heights in post-order and track the best bend seen:

```python
def diameter(root):
    best = 0
    def height(node):
        nonlocal best
        if node is None:
            return -1
        hl = height(node.left)
        hr = height(node.right)
        # path bending at this node
        best = max(best, hl + hr + 2)
        return 1 + max(hl, hr)
    height(root)
    return best
```

In the code, `hl + hr + 2` is the path bending at the current node, and returning −1 for None makes a leaf contribute 0 edges, as it should. This is the archetype of "return one thing, track another": the function *returns* the height (useful to the parent) but *records* the diameter (useful only globally).

> [!warning] The O(n²) version
> Computing `height(left) + height(right)` separately at every node recomputes heights from scratch, which is O(n²) on a chain of n nodes (about half the square of the node count in descendant visits). Combining both in one post-order pass keeps it O(n).

## Key takeaways
- A longest path can bend below the root.
- Return height to the parent while recording the best two-sided path.
- Avoid recalculating full subtree heights at every node.

## Further reading
- [Tree traversal — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tree_traversal)

questions.prompt:
A colleague computes the diameter like this, and analyses it on a left chain of 100,000 nodes, ignoring Python recursion limits. What is its time complexity on that chain?

```python
def diam(node):
    # Handle a missing child first.
    if node is None:
        return 0
    through = (height(node.left) +
               height(node.right) + 2)
    return max(through,
               diam(node.left),
               diam(node.right))
```

(`height` is the lesson's recursive height.)

options.explanation: Every node is visited by `diam`, but at each one `height` re-walks the entire subtree below it.

options.explanation: On a balanced tree this would be O(n log n). On a chain the subtree under each node is not halved; it is all the remaining nodes.

options.explanation: Correct. Each node recomputes the height of its entire remaining chain: 99,999 nodes, then 99,998, and so on. Those walks add up to about half the square of the node count, roughly five billion visits.

options.text: O(2ⁿ), because it recurses twice per node
options.explanation: It does recurse twice, but each node is the root of one `diam` call; the cost comes from the repeated `height` walks, which is polynomial.

1. There is one nonempty diam call per node, plus one more call on None than nodes.
2. At the node with k nodes below it, `height(node.left)` walks all k of them.
3. Add the walks up: 99,999 + 99,998 + … + 1 + 0. That sum is about half the square of the node count, about five billion visits for 100,000 nodes: quadratic, O(n²).
4. (Also, recursion depth 100,000 would hit Python's recursion limit first.)

The lesson's version computes height and diameter **in the same post-order pass**, returning height and recording the best bend: O(n).

lessons.title: Root-to-leaf and downward prefix sums
lessons.summary: A root-to-leaf test must verify that its endpoint is a leaf.
lessons.body:
Use the binary Node with val, left and right fields introduced earlier. Assume a finite acyclic tree with no shared nodes or concurrent mutation. Throughout this unit n counts nodes and h is the tree height in edges. Recursive examples are limited by Python call depth; arithmetic has unit cost and hash-table operations have expected constant cost. Each example distinguishes working storage from returned output.

## Path sums

Three questions with similar names and different techniques.

### Root-to-leaf sum: pass state down

"Is there a root-to-leaf path summing to target?" Subtract as you descend; check at the leaves.

```python
def has_path_sum(node, target):
    if node is None:
        return False
    # Carry the unmet sum toward the leaves.
    r = target - node.val
    # Only an actual leaf may finish this
    # path.
    if not node.left and not node.right:
        return r == 0
    return (has_path_sum(node.left, r) or
            has_path_sum(node.right, r))
```

The leaf check matters: without it, a node with one child could "succeed" at its empty side, counting a path that does not end at a leaf.

### Any downward path: prefix sums

"How many downward paths (starting anywhere, ending anywhere below) sum to target?" Checking every start node is O(n²) on a chain of n nodes. Instead, borrow the **prefix-sum** trick from arrays. Keep the running total from the root down to each node; a downward segment's sum is then a difference of two running totals:

```formula reference
S = R(v) − R(u)
where
v: the node where the segment ends (the current node)
u: an ancestor of v; the segment runs from just below u down to v
R(v): the running sum: the total of all values from the root down to v, inclusive
R(u): the running sum from the root down to u
S: the sum of the values on the segment below u down to v
In words: the sum of a downward segment is the running total where it ends minus the running total just above where it starts.
```

So a downward segment ending at the current node hits the target exactly when some ancestor's running total equals the current running total minus the target. For example, on the path 10 → 5 → 3 with target 8, the running totals are 10, 15 and 18. At node 3, 18 − 8 = 10 is the running total at the root, so the segment 5 → 3 sums to 8. In the code, `run` is the running total at the current node and `seen` counts the running totals on the current path from the root.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: odometer readings on a journey
> On a road trip you note the odometer at every stop. The distance between any two stops is simply the later reading minus the earlier one. To ask "did any stretch of this trip end here and cover exactly 80 km?", you look for an earlier reading that is 80 less than the current one.
>
> **How it maps:** the odometer reading at a stop is the running total from the root, a stretch between stops is a downward segment, and your list of earlier readings is the `seen` map. Turning back to try a different branch means crossing those branch readings off the list, which is the backtrack step.
>
> **Where it stops:** an odometer only goes up. Tree values can be negative or zero, so several ancestors can share the same running total, which is why `seen` counts how many times each total appears rather than just recording it.

```python
from collections import defaultdict

def count_paths(root, target):
    seen = defaultdict(int)
    seen[0] = 1            # empty prefix
    def dfs(node, run):
        if node is None:
            return 0
        run += node.val
        # Matching ancestor prefixes start
        # paths.
        n = seen.get(run - target, 0)
        seen[run] += 1
        n += dfs(node.left, run)
        n += dfs(node.right, run)
        # Remove this prefix
        # before sibling work.
        seen[run] -= 1     # backtrack
        if seen[run] == 0:
            del seen[run]
        return n
    return dfs(root, 0)
```

The **backtrack** line is essential: the map must only contain prefixes on the *current* path, so a node's prefix is removed when the recursion leaves it. Without it, sums from a sibling branch leak in. Removing zero-count entries keeps O(h + 1) distinct active prefixes for a tree of height h; expected time is O(n) for n nodes with constant-cost integer arithmetic and hashing.

## Key takeaways
- A root-to-leaf test must verify that its endpoint is a leaf.
- Prefix differences count segments that start below an ancestor.
- Backtrack prefix counts so sibling branches do not contaminate each other.

## Further reading
- [Tree traversal — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tree_traversal)

questions.prompt:
This root-to-leaf path sum check has no leaf test. What does `bad(root, 1)` return for a root of value 1 with a single **left** child of value 2?

```python
def bad(node, t):
    # Handle a missing child first.
    if node is None:
        return t == 0
    # The leaf test is missing.
    t -= node.val
    return (bad(node.left, t) or
            bad(node.right, t))
```

options.text: False, because the only root-to-leaf path sums to 3
options.explanation: That's the correct answer to the question being asked, but not what this code returns: it accepts reaching *any* None, including the root's missing right child.

options.text: True, because the root's empty right side is reached with a zero remaining target
options.explanation: Correct. After subtracting 1, the remaining target is zero. The left branch fails (the remaining target becomes minus two), but the right child is None and `0 == 0` is True. The 'path' 1 alone doesn't end at a leaf.

options.text: It raises an AttributeError on None
options.explanation: The None check comes first, so `node.val` is never read on None.

options.text: True, because 1 + 2 = 3 is close enough
options.explanation: The comparison is exact: t == 0. The True comes from the empty right side, not from the real path.

questions.workedExample:
1. bad(root=1, t=1), where t is the code's remaining target: t becomes 0.
2. In the left recursive call on value 2 with a zero target, the remaining target becomes minus two; both of 2's children are None, and `-2 == 0` is False. Returns False.
3. In the right recursive call on None with a zero target, the code returns `0 == 0`, **True**.
4. So `bad` returns True, but the only root-to-leaf path is 1 → 2 with sum 3.

The fix is to check for a leaf before recursing, as the lesson's `has_path_sum` does: a None child means 'no path this way', not 'path ended successfully'.

questions.prompt: In `count_paths`, what goes wrong if you delete the backtracking line `seen[run] -= 1`? Consider a root 1 with left child 2 and right child 5, and target 3.

options.text: Nothing; the answer is still 1
options.explanation: Without backtracking the left child's prefix sum (3) stays in the map while the right branch runs, and it gets matched there.

options.text: It returns 0, because prefixes are counted before they are added
options.explanation: The order of 'look up, then add' is fine; the problem is prefixes that are never removed.

options.text: It recurses forever
options.explanation: The recursion is driven by the tree structure, not the map, so it still terminates.

options.text: It returns 2, counting a 'path' that jumps from the left branch to the right
options.explanation: Correct. At node 5 the running sum is 6, and 6 − 3 = 3 was left in the map by the sibling node 2. That matches a non-existent path; the true answer is 1 (1 → 2).

questions.workedExample:
With backtracking, only prefixes on the current ancestor path are active:

| Visit | Running total | Matching prefixes | What changes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Node 1 | 1 | None | Store total 1 |
| Node 2 | 3 | Empty prefix 0 | Count one path; store total 3 |
| Leave node 2 | 3 | — | Remove its total 3 |
| Node 5 | 6 | None | Total 3 is no longer active |

The total is one valid path, through nodes 1 and 2. Without backtracking, the prefix total from node 2 remains active when node 5 is visited. It produces an extra false match, so the flawed total is **2**. Prefix counts must represent the current root-to-node path; otherwise a supposed path combines nodes from different sibling branches.

lessons.title: Maximum path sums with one-sided gains
lessons.summary: Clamp a negative extension to zero rather than taking it.
lessons.body:
Use the binary Node with val, left and right fields introduced earlier. Assume a finite acyclic tree with no shared nodes or concurrent mutation. Throughout this unit n counts nodes and h is the tree height in edges. Recursive examples are limited by Python call depth; arithmetic has unit cost and hash-table operations have expected constant cost. Each example distinguishes working storage from returned output.

## Maximum path sum: post-order with clamping

"Largest sum over any path" (values may be negative). At each node, a path can bend here using the best **downward gain** from each side, but it can only pass **one** side up to the parent, because a path cannot fork. Negative gains are clamped to 0: if extending down a side would lower the sum, just don't extend that way.

So each node does two things:

- **Records a candidate answer**: its own value plus both clamped gains, the best path that bends here.
- **Returns its gain** to its parent: its own value plus the *better* of the two clamped gains, the best path that starts here and goes down one side.

For example, a node of value 2 whose children are leaves of value 1 and 3 records a bend of 2 + 1 + 3 = 6, and offers its parent a one-sided gain of 2 + 3 = 5. If the 1 were −1 instead, the left gain would be clamped to 0 and the bend would be 2 + 0 + 3 = 5.

```python
def max_path_sum(root):
    if root is None:
        raise ValueError("empty tree")
    best = float('-inf')
    def gain(node):
        nonlocal best
        if node is None:
            return 0
        # Ignore extensions that
        # reduce the sum.
        l = max(gain(node.left), 0)
        r = max(gain(node.right), 0)
        best = max(best, node.val + l + r)
        return node.val + max(l, r)
    gain(root)
    return best
```

Initialise `best` to minus infinity (`float('-inf')`, smaller than any number), not 0: in a tree of all-negative values the answer is the largest single node, which is negative. Same shape as diameter: return the one-sided gain, record the two-sided best.

## Key takeaways
- Clamp a negative extension to zero rather than taking it.
- Pass only one downward side to a parent because a path cannot fork.
- Initialise the global best below all values to handle all-negative trees.

## Further reading
- [Tree traversal — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tree_traversal)

     4    5
    / \

options.explanation: Correct. The best path is 6 → 4 → −3 → 5: 6 + 4 − 3 + 5 = 12. Including −2 would only lower it.
10 is the best path within the left subtree (6–4), which is the running best before the root is processed. Bending at the root does better.
15 adds every positive value (4 + 5 + 6), but those three plus −3 are the only way to connect them, and that path is 12.
7 might come from −3 + 4 + 6 (choosing only one side at the root), but at the bend point a path can use both sides.

1. Leaves −2, 6 and 5 have no children, so each one's gain and bend equal its own value: −2, 6 and 5.
2. Node 4: the left gain −2 clamps to 0 and the right gain is 6. Bend: 4 + 0 + 6 = 10. Gain passed up: 4 + 6 = 10.
3. Root −3: left gain 10, right gain 5. Bend: −3 + 10 + 5 = **12**. (Its own gain, −3 + 10 = 7, would only matter to a parent.)
4. The best bend recorded anywhere, the largest of −2, 6, 10, 5 and 12, is **12**: the path 6 → 4 → −3 → 5.

Note the root's own value is negative, but bending through it still pays off because both sides bring positive gains.

lessons.title: Serialising trees with empty-child markers
lessons.summary: Values alone omit shape; empty-child markers make shape explicit.
lessons.body:
Use the binary Node with val, left and right fields introduced earlier. Assume a finite acyclic tree with no shared nodes or concurrent mutation. Throughout this unit n counts nodes and h is the tree height in edges. Recursive examples are limited by Python call depth; arithmetic has unit cost and hash-table operations have expected constant cost. Each example distinguishes working storage from returned output.

## Serialise and deserialise

To send a tree over a network or save it to disk you must flatten it so it can be rebuilt **exactly**. A traversal of values alone is not enough: the trees `1 → left 2` and `1 → right 2` both have pre-order `1, 2`. The fix is to record the **empty children** too.

```
        3
       / \
      9   20
         /  \
        15   7

pre-order with '#' for None:
3,9,#,#,20,15,#,#,7,#,#
```

```python
def serialise(root):
    out = []
    def pre(node):
        if node is None:
            # Record shape,
            # not merely
            # values.
            out.append('#')
            return
        out.append(str(node.val))
        pre(node.left)
        pre(node.right)
    pre(root)
    return ','.join(out)

def deserialise(data):
    tokens = iter(data.split(','))
    def build():
        # Consume exactly this
        # subtree's tokens.
        t = next(tokens)
        if t == '#':
            return None
        node = Node(int(t))
        # Consume the left shape before the
        # right.
        node.left = build()
        node.right = build()
        return node
    root = build()
    if next(tokens, None) is not None:
        raise ValueError("trailing tokens")
    return root
```

This teaching format supports integer node values. Truncated input raises StopIteration, invalid integer text raises ValueError, and extra tokens are rejected; untrusted input also requires size and depth limits. Runtime and storage depend on encoded character length, not just node count.

Deserialising consumes the tokens in the same pre-order they were written, so each recursive call knows exactly where its subtree begins and ends. A tree of n nodes produces one value per node plus **one more null marker than nodes**, because a binary tree always has one more empty child slot than nodes (the binary-counting unit). The example string `3,9,#,#,20,15,#,#,7,#,#` has 5 values and 6 markers. A count that does not match is a quick sign of a truncated or corrupted string.

Level-order with nulls (the format LeetCode displays) works too. A JSON or Protocol Buffers schema can encode nested child relationships explicitly; the format alone does not choose a tree representation.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: dictating a seating plan
> You read a theatre seating plan down the phone, seat by seat in a fixed order. If you only read out names, the listener cannot tell where the gaps are and seats everyone too far forward. Saying "empty" for each empty seat lets them rebuild the plan exactly.
>
> **How it maps:** names are node values, "empty" is the `#` marker, and the fixed reading order is the pre-order walk. The listener fills seats in the same order the plan was read, as `deserialise` consumes tokens in pre-order.
>
> **Where it stops:** a theatre has a fixed grid, so the listener knows how many seats there are. A tree's shape is not known in advance; the markers are the only record of where each branch ends.

## Key takeaways
- Values alone omit shape; empty-child markers make shape explicit.
- Read tokens in the same recursive order as they were written.

lessons.body:
Use the binary Node with val, left and right fields introduced earlier. Assume a finite acyclic tree with no shared nodes or concurrent mutation. Throughout this unit n counts nodes and h is the tree height in edges. Recursive examples are limited by Python call depth; arithmetic has unit cost and hash-table operations have expected constant cost. Each example distinguishes working storage from returned output.

## Constructing a tree from traversals

Given traversals **without** null markers, when can you rebuild the tree? With **distinct** values:

| Given | Unique tree? |
|---|---|
| Pre-order + in-order | Yes |
| Post-order + in-order | Yes |
| Pre-order + post-order | Only if full |
| Pre-order alone | No (but yes for a BST) |

In-order is the key: once you know the root, its position in the in-order sequence tells you exactly which values are in the left and right subtrees. Pre-order tells you the root (its first element), then the left subtree's root, and so on.

```
preorder: 3 | 9 | 20 15 7
inorder:  9 | 3 | 15 20 7
          L  root   R
```

```python
def build_tree(preorder, inorder):
    if len(preorder) != len(inorder):
        raise ValueError("length mismatch")
    pos = {v: i for i, v
           in enumerate(inorder)}
    if len(pos) != len(inorder):
        raise ValueError("duplicate values")
    if set(preorder) != set(inorder):
        raise ValueError("values differ")
    it = iter(preorder)
    def build(lo, hi):     # inorder[lo:hi]
        if lo >= hi:
            return None
        node = Node(next(it))
        mid = pos[node.val]
        if not lo <= mid < hi:
            raise ValueError("bad order")
        # Preorder lists left before right.
        node.left = build(lo, mid)
        node.right = build(mid + 1, hi)
        return node
    return build(0, len(inorder))
```

For distinct hashable values with consistent equality, the dictionary gives expected O(1) index lookup. For n values, the build takes expected O(n) time and O(n) auxiliary dictionary/set space plus the returned nodes; invalid traversal pairs raise an error. The left subtree must be built before the right because that is the order pre-order lists them.

Pre-order and post-order alone are ambiguous whenever a node has a single child: `1 → left 2` and `1 → right 2` both give pre-order `1 2` and post-order `2 1`. And a BST *can* be rebuilt from pre-order alone, because sorting the n values supplies its in-order, at O(n log n) comparison cost, where n counts keys; a bounds-based reconstruction can avoid sorting.

## Key takeaways
- In-order splits the values into left and right subtrees once the root is known.
- Distinct values and a value-to-position map enable linear expected work.
- Pre-order and post-order leave one-child directions ambiguous in general.
